title: 蚂蚁CEO韩歆毅谈医生与AI：模型能力越强，人的专业价值越凸显
summary: 在2026蚂蚁阿福医疗健康生态大会上，蚂蚁集团CEO韩歆毅提出AI赋能医疗的四大思考：延伸专业照护至诊室外以提供连续支持；使AI成为医生临床判断的得力助手，通过整合全病程信息与权威循证知识库，辅助而非替代医生决策；将日常诊疗数据沉淀为医学新知识；利用AI促进医学经验传承。他强调，随着模型能力增强，医生的专业价值反而更加凸显，其角色将转变为可信信息的核验者、复杂取舍的解释者及共同决策的推动者。蚂蚁阿...
full_content:
11月22日至23日，2026蚂蚁阿福医疗健康生态大会在广州举行。在“AI赋能下的未来医院”论坛上，蚂蚁集团首席执行官韩歆毅围绕AI与医疗健康领域的结合，提出四个方面的思考：让专业照护走出诊室、给患者连续的健康支持；让AI成为医生临床判断的得力助手；让日常诊疗沉淀为医学新识；让AI帮助医学经验薪火相传。



“这几年，人工智能已走进临床的很多环节——从门诊到病房，从随访到科研。我们需要思考一个根本命题：当AI走进医院、走进患者的日常生活，它到底该怎样服务医学、服务医生、服务患者？”韩歆毅提出。


在他看来，医疗技术的每一份进步，说到底都在回应三个朴素的期待：患者希望照护不间断、有温度；医生希望有一个可靠、顺手的帮手；医院则希望在资源有限的情况下，接住日益增长的健康需求。“蚂蚁阿福的初心，始终与这个方向同频：从临床真实需求出发，一步步打磨工具，希望阿福能够助力医生更好地行医，助力青年医生更好地成长，助力医院更好地组织医疗服务，”韩歆毅表示。


韩歆毅认为，第一，要让专业照护走出诊室，给患者连续的健康支持。他举例称，四川省人民医院肛肠科黄医生，一年约600台手术，过去术后随访靠一张告知单、几句叮嘱，患者回家后很难跟进，现在借助阿福，提前设置术后关键节点，由系统主动询问康复情况，已完成数百例持续随访。


“这些探索才刚刚开始，阿福只是一个支点，真正的杠杆是医院内部的流程再造和多方协同，”韩歆毅说，期待和各家医院一起打通信息链路、理顺流程，让连续照护成为医院能稳定提供的服务能力。


他表示，第二，要让AI真正成为医生临床判断的得力助手，和医生一起应对医疗的复杂性。疾病是动态变化的：症状怎么演变、治疗有什么反应、用药和生活习惯如何相互影响，都会影响最终结果。


具体看，首先帮医生把病程信息串起来，让医生看到“全病程”，而非“单个切片”。其次给医生一个可信赖的循证知识底座。通过打通UpToDate等权威临床资源和核心医学数据库，AI像一个随身、可检索、可溯源的知识库，快速给出有依据的参考，标注证据来源、说明自身局限，让每次辅助都严谨可靠。


“AI在临床上的价值，不应该是替医生做决定，而是让医生的每个决定，都建立在更完整的信息和更扎实的证据上。”韩歆毅表示，模型能力越强，人的专业价值越凸显，医生可以成为可信信息的核验者、复杂取舍的解释者、共同决策的推动者。同时，AI给出的建议要经得起追问，让医生看得懂、查得到、改得了。


第三，让日常诊疗沉淀为医学新识，用真实世界的经验惠及更多患者。韩歆毅表示，AI可以把门诊记录、随访对话中的非结构化信息，自动转化为结构化研究素材，帮医生捕捉容易被忽略的微小变量，从多维数据中发现临床新规律；同时，推动真实世界研究在日常照护中自然完成。“人机协同还有另一面：不只是AI辅助医生，医生的临床经验也在塑造AI，让AI变得更专业可靠。”


他举例称，宁波大学附属妇女儿童医院的章医生，借助蚂蚁阿福针对不同病种、术后康复场景搭建了十余套随访方案。对此，蚂蚁阿福已为医生打造了一站式科研赋能工具，覆盖随访方案设计、数据自动归集、队列筛选匹配到趋势分析等环节，帮医生随时捕捉真实世界中的临床变化，提升科研产出效率。


第四，让AI帮助医学经验薪火相传，助力青年医生扎实成长。韩歆毅分享了两点具体的做法：首先，把资深医师的经验变成可交互、可反复练习的场景。由带教老师确定教学目标，选取脱敏教学病例，AI分步指导。其次，让每次练习都形成有反馈、可衡量的成长闭环。AI梳理完整的推理脉络，指出思路中的跳跃和遗漏；青年医生的薄弱点被清晰识别，训练内容和难度随之动态调整。


“随着经济社会发展，老百姓的健康需求还会持续增长，短期内优质医疗的供给，还赶不上需求的变化。”韩歆毅表示，阿福所有的探索，都指向同一个愿景：照顾好今天的患者，支撑好今天的医生，也帮助今天的年轻医生更快成长为明天的名医。


目前，蚂蚁阿福医生端已上线“医学”和“AI分身”两大AI助手，支持医生借助AI一站式完成患者管理、科研检索，并打通了用户数超1.5亿的蚂蚁阿福APP，实现医患双端的深度融合。


韩歆毅表示，阿福还需要在真实临床场景中反复检验、持续迭代。“期待和各位同行一起，让医生行医更从容，青年医生成长更扎实，医院组织服务更高效，让每一次技术创新，都转化为患者可感知、医生可信赖、医院可持续的真实价值。”

title: 医渡科技2027财年中期盈利6131万元，超400个专科智能体融入医疗场景
summary: 医渡科技发布2027财年中期业绩，截至2026年9月30日止六个月实现收入3.77亿元，同比增长5.3%；期内利润达6131万元，成功扭亏为盈。业务方面，生命科学解决方案收入增长9.1%至2.02亿元，健康管理平台收入增长4.2%，大数据平台贡献1.23亿元。业绩增长得益于医疗AI场景化应用的深化，公司依托YiduCore底座升级新一代数智中心EYWA 6.0，推出医疗数据集精炼平台，提升数据生产...
full_content:
随着医疗人工智能从技术研发走向临床应用，行业竞争正在从模型能力比拼转向真实业务场景中的价值创造。11月22日，医渡科技（2158.HK）发布2027财年中期业绩报告。截至2026年9月30日止六个月，公司实现收入人民币3.77亿元，同比增长5.3%；期内利润达6131万元，去年同期为亏损1576万元，实现扭亏为盈。

 

从业务结构来看，生命科学解决方案实现收入2.02亿元，同比增长9.1%；健康管理平台和解决方案实现收入5264万元，同比增长4.2%；大数据平台和解决方案收入保持稳定，为公司贡献1.23亿元。

 

业绩增长背后，医疗AI产品的场景化应用成为公司业务发展的重要支撑。

 

依托YiduCore核心技术底座，医渡科技不断完善从医疗数据治理、高质量数据集生产到模型开发和智能体应用的技术体系。报告期内，公司新一代数智中心EYWA 6.0完成升级，进一步强化高质量数据资产生产、全域数据编织、医学知识融合及模型场景赋能能力，为医疗机构建设面向大模型时代的AI-ready数据基础设施提供支持。同时，公司推出医疗数据集精炼平台，围绕数据采样、萃取、标注等环节构建自动化生产链路，提升高质量医疗数据集的生产效率。

 

在应用端，公司持续推动医疗智能体进入医院核心业务流程，覆盖临床辅助、循证决策、科研及医院管理等场景。目前，公司已沉淀400余个专科任务智能体。在某医院出院记录生成场景中，病历生成智能体生成内容的实际采纳率达到80%-91.5%，显示出AI工具在特定临床工作流中的应用价值。

 

截至报告期末，医渡科技已累计服务141家中国顶级医院及53家监管机构和政策制定者。在生命科学领域，公司将AI能力应用于临床研究、患者招募及真实世界研究等环节；在健康管理领域，连续六年担任北京普惠健康保主运营平台、连续四年担任深圳惠民保主运营平台，持续推动健康保障与疾病管理服务落地。

title: 国内首个！蚂蚁阿福医生版接入“循证金标准”UpToDate
summary: 11月22日，蚂蚁阿福医生版正式发布PC工作台版本，并接入威科集团循证医学临床决策支持解决方案UpToDate，成为国内首个集成该“循证金标准”功能的AI平台。即日起，全国医护药师可限时免费试用。此次升级实现了手机App与PC端的双端互通布局：移动端侧重便捷接诊与患者管理，PC端则聚焦病历整理、数据分析及PPT生成等复杂任务。阿福医生版打造覆盖诊前、诊中、诊后及科研的全场景AI工作台，提供智能预问...
full_content:
11月22日，蚂蚁阿福医生版发布PC工作台（电脑端）版本，同时接入威科集团循证医学临床决策支持解决方案UpToDate，成为国内首个接入该专业功能的AI平台。即日起，全国医生、护士及药师等卫生专业技术人员都可通过阿福医生版限时免费试用UpToDate。


此次升级，阿福医生版实现了手机App加PC工作台的双端布局，医生既可以便捷地在手机上借助阿福在线接诊、管理和沟通患者，也能在电脑上借助阿福的AI工具完成整理病历、分析数据、生成医学PPT等较复杂任务，双端打通使用起来更方便。


“阿福期待成为医生临床判断的得力助手，和医生一起应对医疗的复杂性。”蚂蚁集团CEO韩歆毅在当天的论坛上表示。他强调，AI在临床上的价值，不是替医生做决定，而是让医生的每个决定，都建立在更完整的信息和更扎实的证据上。



长期以来，医生面临较高的工作负荷，日常诊疗之外，还要进行大量病历书写、患者随访等工作，部分医生同时承担科研教学任务。如何减少重复性工作、提高工作效率，是医生在繁忙工作中的普遍需求。


基于医生工作需要，阿福医生版打造了覆盖诊前、诊中、诊后及科研的全场景医生AI工作台，帮助医生减负提效，把更多时间留给诊疗和判断。


8月阿福医生版手机APP上线时，提供AI分身助手与AI医学助手，并与1.5亿用户的蚂蚁阿福用户端打通，支持问诊、患者管理及科研检索。此次阿福医生版的PC工作台版本与手机App实现互联互通，可调取病历文书、随访记录等信息，提供智能病历生成、AI临床决策、循证医学回答、医学科研绘图、论文写作助手等12大医学技能。


医生使用阿福医生版PC工作台


在患者诊疗全周期，阿福医生版能为医生提供全程AI辅助。诊前，AI 预问诊可智能追问和总结，让医生接诊更轻松。诊中，AI 总结患者对话，提供专业回复建议，减少医生文书书写负担，AI医学助手助力临床决策更扎实。诊后，医生可通过自己的AI分身设置患者随访计划，跟进患者后续恢复、用药情况，主动提醒复查、提示异常，成为连接医患、延续院外照护的可靠纽带。


此外，阿福还创新推出“AI问答+医生把关”功能，用户在蚂蚁阿福上获得专业AI解答，医生通过阿福医生版进行把关和沟通，以此提升诊疗效率、服务更多患者。


医生使用阿福医生版管理随访患者


越来越多的医生，正在通过阿福医生版更新工作模式、减负增效。


四川省某三甲医院肛肠科副主任医师介绍，过去患者做完手术，他会用A4纸打印注意事项，但患者回家后未必记得，医生也难以逐一联系。现在，他在阿福医生版上设置了一套术后随访计划，系统在患者术后重要节点自动发送消息、总结恢复情况。从10月到11月初，他已通过阿福医生版随访数百位患者，患者满意度、好评度均有提升。


据了解，为进一步融入临床工作流，阿福医生版还在部分医院试点院内版本，探索与医院信息系统、电子病历系统连接，解决医生跨平台工作带来的繁琐。



值得注意的是，为更好辅助医生临床诊断与科研，蚂蚁阿福成为国内首个与威科集团就临床决策支持解决方案UpToDate 达成合作的AI平台。即日起通过阿福医生版的手机电脑双端，全国医生、护士及药师等卫生专业技术人员均可限时免费试用UpToDate。此次合作，是双方继2026年8月威科旗下国际医学期刊入驻阿福医生版之后的又一次合作拓展。


不管是遇到疑难病例需要查询治疗建议，还是了解用药注意事项与禁忌，医生在蚂蚁阿福医生版中通过文字或语音提问，阿福将依托UpToDate，帮助医生快速获得最新、循证的临床指导，并给出可追溯的来源，方便医生查阅相关建议背后的证据质量与推荐强度，结合患者的实际情况作出临床判断。


威科UpToDate素有 “循证医学金标准”之称，内容由全球7600多名临床专家撰写和审核，并跟踪医学新进展进行持续更新，目前已服务全球180多个国家和地区的医学专业人士。阿福医生版本次引入UpToDate全球公认的高品质循证内容，为医生提供专业、易用的AI医学助手，让专业医学知识的检索更加便捷。


阿福医生版上线UpToDate，手机电脑双端可用


威科集团副总裁、威科医学国际市场总经理 Christian Cella表示：“作为聚焦中国医疗健康领域的专业AI平台，蚂蚁阿福率先实现了患者与医生双端的服务打通。阿福强大的AI能力和平台优势，能与威科集团优质医学资源形成强大协同。通过为更多中国基层医生提供UpToDate临床决策支持，我们能够助力更多患者获得高质量的诊疗服务。在今年8月医学期刊合作的基础上，我们期待进一步深化与蚂蚁集团的合作，以备受全球信赖的医学知识更好地服务中国医生和患者。”


除了引入国际循证医学临床决策支持工具UpToDate，阿福医生版还与中国药品监管数据中心、中华医学会、中华营养学会等国内权威机构和医学知识库合作，汇集了超6000万医学指南、医学文献及超14万药品说明书等专业内容，更贴合中国医生日常诊疗习惯与需求。

title: Electronic health record downtime is a patient safety risk
summary: A major hurricane makes landfall near a metropolitan hospital. The emergency department fills with injured residents, power fluctuates across the region, and ambulances begin arriving from facilities ...
full_content:
A major hurricane makes landfall near a metropolitan hospital. The emergency department fills with injured residents, power fluctuates across the region, and ambulances begin arriving from facilities that have lost critical services.

Then the hospital’s electronic health record (EHR) goes dark. Without a redundant environment, clinicians lose immediate access to medication histories, allergies, laboratory results, diagnostic images, and active orders.

For example, a nurse preparing a dose must rely on paper records that may already be outdated. An emergency physician treating an unconscious patient cannot review prior cardiac diagnoses or recent imaging. Teams moving patients to create capacity must hand off care without a complete record. In the middle of a community crisis, the hospital is forced to manage a second emergency inside its own walls.

This scenario illustrates why continuous EHR availability belongs in the same conversation as infection prevention, medication safety, and emergency preparedness. Hospitals operate around the clock, and the clinical record must remain available whenever care is being delivered. Planned maintenance that routinely removes access may be predictable, but predictability does not remove the risk.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

Downtime changes the conditions of care

Recent research in the American Economic Journal: Economic Policy shows how quickly technology disruption can affect patients. A study of ransomware attacks found that hospital volume fell between 17 percent and 24 percent during the initial week of an attack.

Among patients who were already admitted when an attack began, in-hospital mortality rose between 34 percent and 38 percent. The findings apply to ransomware-related disruption, but they reinforce a broader point. When digital systems fail, the conditions under which clinicians deliver care change immediately.

Separately, a 2025 JAMA Network Open analysis examined network disruptions associated with a faulty cybersecurity software update at 759 U.S. hospitals. Of nearly 1,100 internet-based services evaluated, 21.8 percent supported direct patient care. The disruption affected services involving EHRs, imaging, patient portals, monitoring, transfers, and other operational functions.

The operational consequences of downtime are also substantial. In a 2025 Ponemon Institute survey of U.S. health care IT and security professionals, an average of 72 percent of organizations affected by the cyberattack categories studied reported disruption to patient care. Among respondents whose organizations experienced ransomware, 67 percent reported longer lengths of stay, and 56 percent reported delays in procedures or tests. Respondents estimated that downtime or system-performance delays tied to their most costly recent attack caused approximately $859,000 in lost productivity on average.

Some of the most consequential costs of downtime are harder to calculate. They may include delayed medication, an incomplete clinical decision, pressure on neighboring emergency departments receiving diverted patients, and the emotional burden on clinicians delivering care without familiar information and workflows.

Design continuous availability into the service model

Zero planned downtime depends on an operating model that treats reliability as a continuous responsibility. Under a system-as-a-service approach, the technology provider assumes accountability for the software, hardware, implementation, maintenance, upgrades, and ongoing support required to keep the EHR operating. Bringing these elements together under one service model can reduce gaps in ownership and give health care organizations clearer expectations for system performance over the life of the agreement.

The architecture supporting that model should use redundancy to eliminate single points of failure. If a server, data center, network component, or local utility fails, another component should sustain access to the patient record without requiring clinicians to shift to paper workflows.

Upgrades and routine maintenance should also occur without interrupting clinical operations. Hospitals should evaluate whether a proposed solution has demonstrated this level of reliability in high-acuity, high-security environments and during real-world events, including natural disasters and infrastructure failures.

This approach also changes how reliability is evaluated. Rather than accepting recurring maintenance windows as an unavoidable part of EHR ownership, leaders can require continuous availability as a contractual and operational expectation. Clear accountability, resilient architecture, bundled support, and evidence of performance give hospitals a stronger foundation for protecting clinical workflows, care quality, and patient safety around the clock.

A safer standard for digital care

Hospitals cannot prevent every storm, cyberattack, software defect, or infrastructure failure. However, they can build an environment in which those events are far less likely to separate clinicians from the information required for safe decisions. An approach that combines resilient architecture, clear accountability, bundled support, and demonstrated reliability can make zero downtime an achievable standard for health care operations.

As health care leaders make continuous availability a patient safety standard, the industry can move toward a future in which technology remains dependable through routine maintenance and the most demanding moments of care.

Sandra Johnson is a health care executive.

full_content:
31 岁华人工程师万博雯按 ChatGPT 的建议自行减药后死亡，父母起诉 OpenAI。文章追问通用大模型为何敢给出“要命”的答案，也对比了专业医疗 AI 的边界：知道自己不能做什么。

2026年2月，美国西雅图，31岁的华人女工程师万博雯被发现死于公寓。法医鉴定为癫痫猝死，她体内抗癫痫药物拉莫三嗪的浓度，仅为治疗下限的五分之一。

警察介入调查后发现，她曾咨询ChatGPT如何用药并按照其建议擅自修改了医生诊断的用药剂量。

她至少158次向其表达过对减药的担忧，描述过意识混乱、时间感丧失等症状。但每一次，ChatGPT都告诉她“不用担心”。同时，AI给了她隐瞒的话术。当医生要求做血药浓度检测时，ChatGPT称赞她拒绝检查是“非常有效的规避策略”。

不久前，她的父母在旧金山高等法院起诉OpenAI及CEO奥特曼。98页诉状，写满了无照行医、产品缺陷、未充分警告、不当致死。诉状称，GPT-4o为她设计了一张“25天把每天400毫克减到零”的逐日减药表，没有任何医生开具过这样的方案，而拉莫三嗪的FDA说明书强调“不得骤然停药，任何减量都须在医生指导下逐步进行”。

一个高薪工程师为什么会偏信AI的谗言？而一个被设计来生成文本的系统又凭什么给出了“要命”的答案？

这场死亡背后，还有太多关于AI与医疗的边界值得追问。

万博雯毕业于亚利桑那州立大学计算机专业，在亚马逊做机器学习软件工程师。2022年7月职业移民申请获批，2025年10月1日排期终于轮到，她可以递交转身份申请了。也就在那段时间，她开始想一件事：能不能把药减下来。副作用、体检、将来的生活，这些焦虑她全都告诉了ChatGPT。

从2023年开始用，到2025年，她平均每周和它交换超过1500条消息，一天两百多条。

高浓度的AI聊天降低了她的警惕性，所以当她想要自行减药时，第一时间也是问AI。而为什么ChatGPT会给出如此荒谬的诊断建议？

这还要从通用大模型的特征说起。

通用大语言模型的生成逻辑是根据上下文预测最可能出现的下一个词。它优化的目标是“生成一段连贯、可信、让用户满意的回应”。当一个焦虑的人反复问“我能不能减药”，模型在训练中见过的无数对话模式会告诉它：给出一个明确的、可执行的方案，比说“请咨询医生”更“有用”。于是它制定了一份25天减到零的计划，语气笃定，步骤清晰，像一个负责任的顾问。

一项发表在《柳叶刀数字健康》的研究发现，大语言模型在面对包装成临床语言的虚假信息时，受骗率高达46%，而当同样的虚假信息以网络帖子的随意口吻呈现时，受骗率只有9%。模型学会了“临床语言等于可信信息”的模式，却从不核查内容是否真实。万博雯收到的那句“你完全没有必要担心”，在语言概率上是一句自然的回应。在医学事实方面，它是一个没有行医资质的系统对癫痫患者做出的可能导致死亡的判断。

而另一方面，媒体的渲染也加强了群体对AI的盲从与偏信。过去几年，AI医疗的公共叙事经历了一轮持续的升温。硅谷CEO在社交平台上宣称AI能在五到十年内治愈大多数人类疾病。短视频里，AI数字人穿着白大褂、挂着胸牌，以“医务工作者”形象推荐药品，声称“亲测有效”。科技媒体上，“手搓mRNA疫苗救回患癌爱犬”“车库实验室研发出阿尔茨海默候选新药”的故事反复刷屏。

这给了公众一种错觉：AI正在让医疗平权成为现实，而智能就是万能药。再加上AI大模型自身带有的谄媚特质，这场悲剧便发生了。

万博雯的悲剧里，有一个问题始终没有被回答：她为什么不去问医生？

医生给她开了拉莫三嗪，医嘱写着“逐步减量须在医生指导下进行”。但当她担心副作用、担心药物影响面试表现时，打开的是ChatGPT的对话框。对一个正在焦虑中等待的人来说，AI的即时回应比医生的审慎更能缓解焦虑。

这就引出了一个必须回答的问题：如果她用的不是ChatGPT，而是一款专业医疗AI，结局会不会不同？

答案很可能不是一份减药计划。专业医疗AI的设计逻辑里，有一条通用模型从未被写入的规则：当问题触及用药调整、剂量变更、停药决策时，系统的正确回应应该是“拒绝给出方案，并把你推向能承担责任的人”。

以“蚂蚁阿福”为例。这个医疗AI助手总用户数已突破1亿，连接了全国5000多家医院和30万真人医生。它的定位从一开始就很清楚：健康问答、报告解读、就医引导。

当用户的问题超出健康管理范畴、进入临床决策领域时，阿福的设计是把人引向真人医生，而不是自己给出一个笃定的答案。蚂蚁集团在发布时明确说过，阿福的回答“并非医疗诊断，也永远不会替代真人医生”。国家卫健委《卫生健康行业人工智能应用场景参考指引》中出现频率最高的两个词是“智能”和“辅助”，定位同样是辅助工具，而非替代。

再看监管层面的数据。截至2025年10月，国家药监局已批准超过110款基于深度学习的第三类医疗器械独立软件产品，用途集中在辅助分诊、辅助识别与检测等特定场景。三类证是中国医疗器械的最高级别认证，意味着产品经过严格的临床验证和审评。而这些拿到三类证的产品，没有一款的用途是“为患者制定用药调整方案”。它们的共同特征是：能力范围窄、适用场景明确、有医生作为最终决策者。窄不是缺陷，是安全设计的一部分。窄意味着每一句输出都能追溯到临床证据，每一个建议背后都有人或制度兜底。

这就引出了这一节要说的核心：专业AI的安全来自“知道自己不能做什么，并且把用户往能做的人那里推”；通用AI的风险来自“不知道自己不该做什么，并且把用户留在对话里”。专业AI的价值恰恰在于它知道自己看不了病，所以链接了真人医生。

万博雯需要的从来不是一个更聪明的模型。她需要的，是一个在她问出“我能不能减药”的时候，能识别出这是高风险临床决策，然后说“这个问题我不能回答，请你联系你的神经科医生”的系统。

万博雯的事件是否意味着AI对医学一无是处呢？

并非如此，模型还是可以回答很多医学问题，只是使用者需要保持审慎。全球每周有数十亿条与健康相关的问询涌向这类模型，超过八亿活跃用户里，每四个人就有一个每周会提健康问题。

对于普通人，可以记住几件很具体的事：

首先，选专用工具，而不是万能工具。查症状、看药品说明书、理解检查报告，优先用有明确医学语料来源、答案带引用且被设计为“转介医生”而非“替代医生”的专业医疗AI产品，而不是把通用聊天大模型当成全科大夫。通用模型的优势是什么都能聊，而这恰恰是它在医疗场景里最不该有的特性。

其次，把它当搜索引擎用，不当诊断者用。可以问“拉莫三嗪常见副作用有哪些”“突然停药会发生什么”，这类问题有标准答案。不要问“我这个情况能不能减到零”这类需要研究病史的内容。

并且尤其要警惕这几类对话。一是给你具体剂量、具体天数、具体停药方案的；二是把你的异常症状解释为“正常反应”“正在好转”的；三是让你对医生保密或暗示医生“不了解你的特殊情况”的。任何让你远离医生的建议都值得被当成危险信号。

其实，临床AI上有个很实用的习惯：把想问AI的问题抄下来，原样带去门诊。让AI帮你列一份问医生的提纲梳理自己的问题。

这起悲剧也为行业和监管敲响了警钟。规范AI医疗助手，必须坚守以下底线：第一，在未通过医疗安全认证的部分疾病前，严禁AI替代医生给出实质性的诊疗建议；第二，遇到任何涉及用药剂量的提问，必须明确拒绝并建议患者咨询专业医生；第三，必须在产品内显著提示，AI提供的健康信息不可替代专业医疗诊断、仅供参考。

生命只有一次，在医学问诊这样重要的领域里，比起AI，我们更应该相信医生的判断。

title: Cash flow, not revenue, keeps a private practice independent
summary: Independent medical practices play an important role in health care. They offer physicians the opportunity to shape clinical decisions, build lasting patient relationships, and operate with a degree o...
full_content:
Independent medical practices play an important role in health care. They offer physicians the opportunity to shape clinical decisions, build lasting patient relationships, and operate with a degree of autonomy that can be difficult to achieve in larger organizations. Yet independence also brings financial responsibilities that have little to do with diagnosing or treating patients. A physician can run a busy schedule and still struggle to maintain predictable cash flow.

That distinction matters. A practice may be clinically successful without being financially resilient. When expenses rise faster than payments arrive, owners may postpone hiring, delay equipment upgrades, or spend time solving administrative problems that compete with patient care. Financial stability is not separate from a practice’s mission; it helps make that mission sustainable.

The gap between revenue and available cash

The distinction between services rendered, income accrued, and money collected is one of the most typical sources of confusion. The medical practice might render a large number of services before the money comes from the insurance companies or the patients. All at the same time, payroll, rent, technology subscriptions, and other obligations go as scheduled. Therefore, a financially successful month may go hand in hand with having a lack of money in the bank.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

It is essential to evaluate the process of payment collection, fixed costs, and the amount of money necessary to run the practice during slow periods for doctors. This evaluation is especially relevant when new hires or expansion of the medical practice is expected. Projections of revenue increase can be helpful, but the moment of collecting the money will play an essential role.

Consider a hypothetical practice expecting to add a clinician. The additional appointments may ultimately increase revenue, but the practice could face months of salary, credentialing, and onboarding costs before the new clinician reaches a full schedule. A plan based only on future billings would overlook the cash needed during that transition.

Making investment decisions with a clear purpose

Equipment, office improvements, and expanded services can improve a practice’s capabilities. Still, not every desirable investment should be made immediately. Owners should distinguish between investments required to maintain safe, effective operations and those intended to support future growth. Each deserves a realistic estimate of its total cost, expected benefit, and effect on cash flow.

For example, purchasing diagnostic equipment may involve more than the quoted purchase price. Installation, staff training, maintenance, and software costs can change the economics. Expanding office space may introduce additional rent, insurance, utilities, and administrative expenses long before patient volume catches up. Understanding the full commitment helps physicians avoid confusing the ability to purchase something with the ability to afford it over time.

Financing can be one tool for managing these costs. Depending on the purpose and eligibility requirements, a practice may consider conventional business financing, government-backed small-business programs, an equipment loan, or a line of credit. These options serve different needs. Long-term investments may be better matched to structured repayment, while short-term timing gaps require particular care so that temporary borrowing does not become permanent dependence.

The lowest monthly payment is not necessarily the least expensive choice. Owners should compare total borrowing costs, fees, collateral requirements, repayment flexibility, and any personal guarantees. Most importantly, they should ask whether the investment remains manageable if revenue falls below expectations.

Protecting independence through preparation

Financial planning does not need to begin with a complex forecast. A useful starting point is a monthly review of cash on hand, accounts receivable, operating expenses, debt payments, and upcoming capital needs. Owners can then test a few reasonable scenarios: What if collections arrive later than expected? What if a key employee leaves? What if a new service takes longer to become established? The purpose is not to predict every setback, but to understand the practice’s room to respond.

A separate operating reserve can provide flexibility when expenses are unexpected or payments are delayed. The appropriate amount will vary with the practice’s size, specialty, staffing, and revenue cycle. Physicians should also involve their accountant and other qualified advisers before making a significant acquisition, borrowing decision, or expansion commitment. Sound financial information is especially valuable when a physician is balancing the practice’s needs against personal obligations such as retirement savings and household expenses.

Independent ownership can offer meaningful rewards, but it also concentrates responsibility. The physician-owner must consider the financial consequences of decisions that might otherwise be handled by a hospital system or corporate office. That responsibility becomes more manageable when financial planning is treated as a regular part of practice operations rather than an emergency response.

Ultimately, financial stability is not about maximizing borrowing or avoiding every expense. It is about maintaining enough flexibility to make thoughtful clinical and business decisions. A practice with a clear understanding of its cash flow, measured investment priorities, and realistic contingency plans is better positioned to care for patients while preserving the independence its owner worked to build.

This article is for general educational purposes only and does not constitute financial, legal, tax, or professional advice. Financing options and terms depend on individual circumstances and applicable requirements. Physicians should consult qualified advisers before making significant business decisions.

Chris Cornella is a health care executive.

title: 三十年功能仿真积累，心运医疗给出心脏数字孪生的“中国答案”
summary: 心运医疗依托浙江大学夏灵教授团队三十余年心脏功能仿真积累，由创始人邓冬东博士领衔，给出心脏数字孪生的“中国答案”。公司成立于2022年，构建“科研攻坚、产业落地”双核架构，针对欧美技术未覆盖的本土人群疾病特征进行验证。其核心技术壁垒在于“心脏数字孪生模型重建及电生理仿真技术”，区别于仅复刻结构的传统三维重建，该技术能深入模拟心肌电生理特性，通过患者磁共振图像重建个体化模型，精准定位导致室速、房颤的...
full_content:
1990年代，个人电脑尚未普及，浙江大学夏灵教授已经在计算机里“搭建”心脏了。

 

没有现成软件，也没有足够算力，他用一行行代码模拟心肌细胞的电活动，试图让一颗虚拟心脏像真的一样跳动、传导，甚至发生心律失常。

 

夏灵教授专注虚拟心脏三十多年，先后主持7项国家自然科学基金项目，发表150多篇论文，成为国内数字仿真领域绕不开的专家。

 

而夏灵教授的学生、心运医疗创始人邓冬东教授，则是这条技术路线的接棒人。

 

在浙江大学生物医学工程专业获得博士学位后，邓冬东赴约翰斯霍普金斯大学心脏仿真团队从事博士后研究，参与全球最早一批个性化心脏建模的临床转化。

 

这段经历让他看清：国际技术虽然先进，围绕的却主要是欧美人群的疾病特征。要让虚拟心脏真正服务中国患者，必须针对本土人群做验证。

 

这也解释了心运医疗为何从一开始就把临床问题放在首位。“我们做了三十多年研究，从一开始就是冲着解决临床问题去的。”邓冬东坦言。

 

推动研究走出实验室的契机，来自产业资本。2022年，杭州心运医疗科技有限公司成立。夏灵教授任首席科学家，邓冬东教授牵头技术研发，公司同时搭起“科研攻坚、产业落地”的双核架构。

 

心运医疗的路径，是把患者的心脏磁共振图像重建成个体化数字模型，输入电生理参数后进行仿真，观察心电传导是否出现折返环。折返环的位置，既提示猝死风险，也指向消融靶点。

 

2026年9月，第九届中国医疗器械创新创业大赛收官，心运医疗凭借“心脏数字孪生技术指导复杂心律失常消融靶点精准定位与心脏性猝死风险评估”项目，拿下医用软件与数字医疗类别赛一等奖和人工智能产品总决赛一等奖，把这项硬核技术推到产业聚光灯下。

 


心运医疗的核心技术是“心脏数字孪生模型重建及电生理仿真技术”。

 

提到心脏数字孪生，行业最常见的误区是把它等同于三维重建或AI影像分析。

 

“市面上很多数字孪生是结构性的，把心脏的样子在电脑里复刻一遍。心律失常不仅与心脏结构异常有关，更与心肌电生理特性的异质性密切相关。心律失常并非单纯的心脏结构或力学问题，还涉及疾病过程中心肌电生理特性的病理性改变。”邓冬东介绍道。

 

心运医疗的壁垒在于功能性仿真：不仅复刻心脏的“形”，还模拟心脏的“电”。

 

要理解“电”为什么关键，得回到折返环。折返环，是心电信号在病变心肌里走错路形成的异常闭环，也是室速、房颤的根源。找到完整的折返环，就能精准消融。

 

心脏数字孪生技术定位的室速折返环（红色箭头标记）

 

但传统电生理标测只能探测心内膜表面，穿透不了心肌深层，“定位难”正源于此。心运医疗的仿真则提供了一条无创、精准的路径：全程不进入体内，在术前锁定折返环，把消融靶点从“术中试”变成“术前算”。

 

具体而言，这套流程在数字世界复现一次真实的心脏电活动：

 

先以深度学习算法自动分割钆增强MRI影像，识别正常心肌、半梗死区与完全梗死区；再插值重建高分辨率三维模型，还原心肌纤维旋向；随后按病因匹配特异性电生理参数，导入心室肌单细胞离子模型；最后由超级计算机完成全心脏电生理仿真，追踪折返环路径，锁定消融靶点。

 

“团队不是靠大数据拟合出概率结果，而是从底层物理机制出发，把患者的心电传导完整演算一遍。”邓冬东强调。

 

这种“机制驱动”路线与主流的“数据驱动”医疗AI有本质区别：它不依赖海量标注做黑盒预测，结果可解释、可复现，也更容易获得医生信任。

 

门槛也正源于此。它不是算法工程师堆代码能跑通的，需要生物医学工程、心脏电生理、临床医学与高性能计算深度交叉，还要长期进行参数调优与临床反馈。

 

邓冬东把护城河归为两样东西：与临床医生几十年积累的参数经验，以及基于信任建立的数据协作网络。

 


基于这套底层技术，心运医疗布局了四条产品线。

 

产品一，心脏性猝死（SCD）风险预测。传统评估主要依赖左心室射血分数，难以准确识别恶性心律失常风险。心运通过患者特异性心脏数字孪生模型，模拟室速诱发及折返环路形成，实现更精准的猝死风险分层。

 

产品二，室性心动过速个性化精准消融靶点定位。复杂室速消融最难的是“找”。心运把逐点标测前移到计算机：术前仿真锁定折返环，模拟不同消融术式，再把方案交给医生。

 

产品三，心脏数字孪生结合立体定向消融放疗，治疗难治性室速。对无法耐受常规手术的患者，心运把仿真靶点导入放疗设备，用体外放射线完成消融，是目前国际上少有的全无创产品线。

 

产品四，心房颤动个性化精准消融靶点定位。房颤机制更复杂，目前仍处建模仿真研究阶段。但房颤会因心房血液淤积显著升高脑梗风险，有效治疗意味着降低中风发生率。

 

“它们是一个既相互联系、又有各自特殊特征的产品管线。”邓冬东说。

 

从SCD风险筛查识别高危患者，到ICD植入后频繁放电的患者接受导管消融，再到无法耐受常规手术的患者转向立体定向放疗，四款产品构成了一条覆盖心律失常不同阶段和术式的产品链条。

 


产品线铺开后，技术行不行，最终靠临床数据说话。

 

目前，心运医疗已完成多例患者的心脏电生理仿真，合作网络覆盖安贞、阜外、解放军总医院、邵逸夫医院等十余家顶级心血管中心。

 

猝死风险预测方向，北京朝阳医院回顾性研究显示：仿真未诱发折返的患者，随访心律失常发生率为0；分层准确率比单靠LVEF提升25倍。

 

 国内第一篇利用个体化心脏建模仿真直接指导临床室速消融的论文，标志着中国在利用个体化心脏建模仿真应用于临床治疗室速患者消融方面已经和国际接轨

 

室速靶点定位方向，2026年7月完成的前瞻性对照研究显示，数字孪生定位的折返环与术中三维标测关键峡部完全一致。这是国内首项个体化建模仿真直接指导临床室速消融的前瞻性验证。

 

最颠覆的突破来自立体定向消融放疗。国际综述显示，全球近300例立体定向放疗一年复发率超80%；心运与解放军总医院合作的十几例患者全程无创，手术总时长约15分钟，实际照射仅5～6分钟，随访最长近两年无复发。

 

“以前医生怕打不准、伤正常心肌。现在术前把靶点锁死，放疗科医生照着靶区打就行。”无创、精准、全面，正从技术描述变成临床数据里的具体事实。

 


技术跑通之后，商业化是必答题。对心运医疗来说，最现实的命题是：全球首创、无同类获批产品可参照，注册路径该怎么走？

 

邓冬东的答案是分步走：先按二类医疗器械申报，以辅助决策工具的身份快速落地，积累真实世界数据与临床共识；等行业认知与监管标准成熟，再升级三类。

 

按规划，心脏影像处理软件预计2027年中拿证；猝死风险预测、室速靶点定位产品2027～2028年陆续启动申报；放疗联合方案也已提上日程。

 

市场定位上，心运选的是一条“互补而非竞争”的路。

 

“我们就像电生理手术的GPS，只负责精准定位病灶，让各类消融手段变得更准、更快、更彻底。”邓冬东说，这套定位模式，为产业链合作留出空间。

 

心运的技术版图也不止于心律失常。团队已经把技术从缺血性心肌病拓展至肥厚型、扩张型心肌病，远期有望延伸到心衰评估、心肌缺血预测等场景，“长期目标是做一个覆盖全心脏疾病的数字孪生平台，贯穿风险预测、术前规划到术后随访。”

 

路并不平坦：注册周期、算力成本、医生认知教育都是现实挑战。为此，公司计划自建超算仿真中心，压降单例算力成本；同时以头部医院为突破口，依靠学术共识逐步向下渗透。

 

从夏灵教授在90年代启动心脏仿真研究，到这套技术走向临床验证，国内心脏仿真研究已经走过三十余年。

 

如今心运医疗要回答的问题，早已不是“能否实现仿真”，而是产品能否顺利注册、进入医院、稳定服务临床。后续的临床验证与注册推进，将一步步检验这项技术真正的临床价值边界。

title: 脑机接口规则，这次中国先行
summary: 中国在脑机接口领域正加速从技术突破转向全球标准制定者角色。近期，我国牵头制定的《信息技术 脑机接口 参考架构》国际标准正式发布，距首项术语国际标准发布仅一年。同时，多项行业标准如脑电数据集质量要求、植入式系统临床试验审评要点相继出台，配合此前发布的术语及性能测试标准，构建起完善的标准体系。此外，全国首个国家脑机接口高质量数据集项目在武汉启动，标志着标准、数据与审评齐头并进。通过发布分类界定、命名指...
full_content:
在脑机接口上，我国已经准备好要做标准制定者了！


最近几个月，我国频繁在脑机接口标准领域发力。今年9月，我国牵头制定的《信息技术 脑机接口 参考架构》（ISO/IEC 27572:2026）由国际标准组织（ISO/IEC）正式发布，距离我国牵头的脑机接口首项国际标准《信息技术 脑机接口 术语》（ISO/IEC 8663:2025）正好一年。


与此同时，YY/T 2029—2026《脑机接口医疗器械用于人工智能算法的脑电数据集质量要求与评价方法》行业标准和《植入式脑机接口手部运动功能代偿系统临床试验技术审评要点》也在近期相继发布。前者是我国第三项脑机接口医疗器械行业标准，此前两项分别为《采用脑机接口技术的医疗器械术语》（YY/T 1987—2025）和《采用脑机接口技术的医疗器械 具备闭环功能的植入式神经刺激器感知与响应性能测试方法》（YY/T 1996—2025）。


更值得一提的是，由华中科技大学同济医学院附属同济医院牵头的全国首个国家脑机接口高质量数据集项目近日也在武汉启动。


标准、数据、审评齐头并进，显然，在脑机接口领域，国内已不满足于技术上的突破，正在剑指全球脑机接口标准话语权。



标准话语权，首先需要定义“脑机接口是什么”，从而决定脑机接口的设计、审评标准。


今年6月，我国先后发布《脑机接口医疗器械产品分类界定指导原则》与《脑机接口医疗器械通用名称命名指导原则》，划定管理属性、类别与命名规则，从而对医疗脑机接口进行了初步界定。


我国牵头的脑机接口首项国际标准《信息技术 脑机接口 术语》则由中国医学科学院生物医学工程研究所专家蒲江波担任项目负责人，联合美、日、澳等8个国家专家共同完成，梳理出基本概念、分类、信号、实验、应用等8大类126个词条，于去年9月正式发布。


在术语标准之外，我国牵头的《信息技术 脑机接口 用例》（ISO/IEC TR 27599:2025）也已于去年5月发布，收录了医疗健康、工业控制、智能环境等领域的代表性用例。


今年8月，首批两项国家标准《信息技术 脑机接口 参考架构》（GB/T 47023—2026）与《信息技术 脑机接口 多模态数据格式》（GB/T 47127—2026）在国内正式实施。其中，参考架构围绕“脑机接口是什么、怎么用、有什么功能、如何实现”四个核心问题，统一了侵入式、半侵入式、非侵入式等不同技术路线的系统组成、功能划分和实现方式，由浙江大学、中国电子技术标准化研究院以及华为、博睿康、强脑科技等企业参与起草。至此，术语、用例、参考架构三项脑机接口基础国际标准均已由中国专家牵头完成。

对于多项标准和指南的密集发布，合盈脑机基金合伙人张宇涛认为，这标志着国内脑机接口行业正从科研原型跨入规范化产业化阶段，试图打造从定义权到审评权的完整闭环：“第一，《ISO/IEC 27572:2026》定义了侵入、半侵入、非侵入的模块与接口逻辑。定义架构就能定未来兼容性。这个我国牵头的国际参考架构标准标志着我们主动参与、主导全球脑机接口顶层定义；第二，《YY/T 2029》作为全球首个AI训练用脑电数据的采集、标注、评价标准，把数据从素材变成可交付物，填补了脑电数据集的标准化空白，解决AI模型训练的数据来源、质量判定问题；第三，植入式BCI手部运动代偿系统审评要点则给侵入式脑机的注册路径划出清晰可落地的边界，规定了有效性因素。”


他更结合投资与估值观察了标准密集落地的影响：“这将会带来赛道估值体系的重大重构。第一，标准划定及格线，不达标或故事炒作的路线和产品会快速出清。估值角度从不确定性折价换成合规溢价，大幅限制概念炒作，转向真正有临床落地能力、符合标准框架的企业。等于说早期项目的估值上限被封顶，但同时，未来腰斩风险也下降了。投资窗口期更为明确，进而产业投资路线清晰，会成为主流方式。第二，估值锚的逻辑会发生切换，从过去项目估值更多看团队背景、实验室论文、样机参数，到未来明确向更清晰的注册路径倾斜，合规能力、标准化临床证据、数据集建设能力将决定估值。短期内，进入创新器械通道并有 IIT数据的公司将拿到溢价。随后，则将会进入批件和例数的分化期，溢价会逐渐转移到谁能放量。”


来自企业的体感更为直接。思昇科技是一家专注于AI驱动的超声脑机接口技术研发与产业化的创新公司，今年5月初步完成核心团队组建，围绕“数据获取-算法解析-仿真验证-临床应用”构建平台化技术与产品布局，首个产品定位为经颅低强度超声介导血脑屏障开放以辅助胶质母细胞瘤治疗。其联合创始人徐宜蕙向动脉网表示，公司自创立起就在持续跟踪脑机接口领域的标准化进展及医疗器械技术审评指导文件。据初步梳理，目前已发布或正在制定的国标、行标、团标及国标计划接近50项。


“这背后反映出一个重要趋势：脑机接口正在从单点技术突破走向系统化发展，行业开始逐步建立共同的技术语言、数据规范和评价框架。其中，脑机接口参考架构、数据集质量要求和评价方法、多模态数据格式以及医疗器械技术审评指导文件等，对企业开展产品定义、技术研发、质量控制和注册路径规划具有重要指导意义。”她也向动脉网介绍了跟踪研究中的发现：“国际上的脑机接口标准大多集中在ISO/IEC JTC1/SC43，偏信息技术领域，传统医疗口的国际标准组织还没发布直接相关的标准。国内则是国家药监局、国家标准委都在牵头推进。我也很期待，我国之后是不是能在医疗这个领域率先在国际上发声，甚至占据主导。”


不过，随着脑机接口技术路线日益多元化，现有标准体系仍有进一步完善的空间。徐宜蕙坦言，当前相关标准和技术审评指导文件主要围绕脑电信号及植入式电极技术展开，尚难以全面覆盖超声脑机接口的技术特点与评价需求。思昇科技正积极推动超声脑机接口相关技术的规范化研究，并加强与临床专家、监管部门等的交流，希望将超声技术的独特需求和实践经验融入相关标准的研究与制定中。



当然，在定义之外。数据也一直是脑机接口稀缺的东西。10月24日启动的国家脑机接口高质量数据集，正是落在这个最稀缺环节的一枚棋子。


根据公开信息，这一全国首个同类项目由同济医院牵头，聚焦脑卒中康复、脊髓损伤、帕金森病、癫痫、意识障碍等10类疾病方向共6种数据模态，将建设脑信号采集、意图解码、功能评估、神经调控、康复交互等多模态数据集，拟于2027年建成投用，形成安全可控的数据流通机制。


脑机行业资深专家Jay Zhu认为这一举措意义重大。他表示，之所以侵入式脑机数据在单一企业体系内的意义较为有限，核心在于数据的价值密度依赖于跨样本的广度与多样性，但单一企业的数据规模不足以支撑泛化能力。


他认为，侵入式脑机接口面临的核心工程瓶颈是个体异质性较大：不同受试者的电极植入位点存在偏差，大脑皮层解剖形态、植入后胶质瘢痕演化特征，以及目标脑区的神经编码模式均存在显著个体差异。这导致算法在A患者身上训练的解码模型，直接迁移到B患者身上往往性能大幅衰减。要突破这一瓶颈，需要尽可能多的汇集多中心、跨设备、跨适应症的高质量数据，训练可提取通用神经编码基元的基座模型，以此提升跨个体迁移能力。


“企业各自封闭数据，每家都只能基于几十例甚至几例数据做局部优化，无法催生行业级的通用解码范式。更关键的是，脑机数据的采集成本极高，封闭使用意味着同一份数据只能被一家企业挖掘一次，社会总回报被严重稀释。数据锁在保险柜里只会随时间贬值，越早汇聚、越早被多方算法反复使用，其科学和商业价值才越大。这也是为什么国家层面推动数据集联盟、强制标准化汇聚，本质上是在着力打破这种各自为战、画地为牢的封闭格局。侵入式脑机国家数据集最核心的价值，在于这一底层基建将有望助推我国脑机产业从与美国并跑升级为领跑。要知道，我国脑疾病患者基数远大于美国，且我国行政驱动的基建速度远超美国。正因此，我国在侵入式脑机临床试验数量上已经开始显著超越美国。Neuralink积累10年公开植入数仅27例，而国内目前接受脑机植入的患者已有200-300人，其中使用时长超一个月且设备仍在体的患者人数根据报道已经超过百人”，Jay Zhu向动脉网解释了公共数据集的重大意义。


“更关键的是，我国将在侵入式脑机领域领跑的驱动逻辑不在于单体项目的技术更强，而是整体的‘患者基数+行政动员能力+临床放量速度’叠加，使数据基建成为临床推进的自然产物，从而形成正循环增长飞轮，快速促进更多项目进入临床、完成临床、超越临床。这也意味着未来筛选项目时，谁更早接入国家数据集联盟、谁的临床数据能进入标准化流通管道，将成为比单纯的电极通道数更关键的指标，从而让项目冒头乃至拔尖”，Jay Zhu进一步补充道。


徐宜蕙则基于自身需求对公共数据集的价值做出了清醒的判断：“公共数据集对我们的价值，更多在于为算法研发提供基础验证、方法学对照和跨模态研究的支撑公共数据集显然是算法验证和跨模态研究的基础和对照。，但现有数据集仍主要围绕脑电及植入式电极信号展开，超声等新兴模态的数据积累和标准化建设相对不足。针对这一现状，以脑电和植入式电极为主，缺少超声企业参与，思昇科技正在探索构建融合真实采集、数值仿真与公共数据的多源数据体系。一方面，依托自主研发的超声硬件，逐步积累声学信号、脑微血流及功能成像等特色临床数据；另一方面，利用经颅超声仿真软件生成不同颅骨结构、脑区靶点及声学参数条件下的仿真数据，并与真实测量数据相互校验、与公共数据集进行关联融合，拓展复杂应用场景下的数据覆盖范围。会用自研硬件补充采集声信号，再做超声仿真数据，与公共数据、临床自采数据综合使用。”


这也引出了一个关于脑机接口企业数据护城河的问题。张宇涛对此表示：“总体来看，脑机接口企业要建立数据护城河需要三个必要条件。一是不可替代的采集场景，比如术中、植入后长期随访；二是标注与参数绑定，非裸信号，是‘参数-响应’的耦合；三是规模随装机量线性增长。同济牵头的国家高质量数据集虽然解决了第一部分，包括多病种多模态及跨院互认，但其无法满足后面两点。公共数据集难以覆盖全部细分场景，比如特定亚型及病例、长期植入后多年随访的脑电信号，这些稀缺、长周期、完整预后随访的数据，依然是企业的核心护城河。”


“这会对项目筛选维度带来重大转变，以前投资人看企业是否有可复制大规模采集脑电的能力，未来则要看企业能否利用公共数据集做算法迭代，同时能否构建独特的垂直私有数据集。如果企业完全依赖公开数据集，自身没有临床积累，算法易被同质化。竞争优势将在于企业能否把公共基础数据和自有稀缺结合，建立闭环的临床数据结合”，他进一步提到了数据带来的脑机接口企业估值重构。


有了数据底座，单点临床突破才可能沉淀为通用能力。



我国最近频繁制定标准的背后，则是脑机接口产业端的热闹。


据公开报道梳理，今年国内脑机接口融资频繁，屡创新高。仅上半年融资总额就超72亿元，已是去年全年3倍的水平。其中，强脑科技完成20亿元融资，创下国内脑机接口最大单笔纪录。此外，阶梯医疗下半年以来完成约14亿元融资，截至9月累计融资已达26亿元。


今年以来，陆续已有博睿康、阶梯医疗和术理创新启动IPO进程。同时，未经证实的消息显示，强脑科技也已秘密在港股提交招股书。


在临床端，多家公司也迎来进展。尤其博睿康在今年3月获得全球首张植入式脑机接口三类医疗器械注册证，并已进入商保支付体系。


更明确的信号来自政策端，脑机接口首次被写入政府工作报告，被列入未来产业方向。


不过，资本热度越高，风险也越大。


Jay Zhu向动脉网分享了他的深入观察：“不少明星项目资本化已进入中后期阶段，动辄数十亿甚至百亿估值，对应的临床落地阶段却是刚完成型检、刚启动人体临床试验、刚完成个位数人体植入的早期阶段。估值锚点还停留在押注团队背景和赛道热度上，这种阶段错配，一旦遭遇临床进度延迟、监管政策收紧或脑机赛道阶段性热度回落，估值回调幅度可能会远超预期。”


张宇涛把支付端列为最大担忧：“同质化与支付缺位叠加，如果数家企业拿证却都无法放量，价格战会先于市场到来。规模化付费需求要等收费编码落地且单例经济为正后出现，预测这个时间点大约在2028-2030年。对于资本而言，退出主通道可能是并购而非IPO，潜在买方包括美敦力、波士顿科学、雅培等跨国器械企业，联影、迈瑞、微创等国内平台公司，以及头部药企。”


他更进一步在参考脑深部电刺激（DBS）和骶神经调控（SNM）的放量历史后，提出了接下来国内脑机接口冲击全球领军地位需要提升的领域：“提升渗透率的不是电极，而是术式培训和程控师职业化。我建议把术者认证及程控师职业写进下一批标准或指南。在输出标准后，输出怎么用这套标准的人的体系化才是关键。同时，还要补上生物材料、医工人才、海外多中心临床和术后随访生态的短板。”


Jay Zhu给出的建议则是临床数据的监管互认：“标准文本不等于数据互认。我国已积累了全球领先的植入例数和随访数据，但整体质量尚未达到被FDA或CE直接采信的水平，企业出海仍要在海外重新做临床。真正的话语权，是我们的本土临床数据被全球主要监管体系认可为有效证据。这一步打通，中国才能从参与者变成规则共建与主导者。”


身处一线的企业对于国内脑机接口行业影响力的提升也感同身受。徐宜蕙表示很明显看到中国在脑机接口领域更有承担力了，获得越来越多国际同行的关注与认可开始被国际同行认可。思昇科技也将顺应这个大潮，尽早更早布局国际标准化工作，推动超声脑机接口相关技术与评价方法融入国际标准体系，同时提前开展海外市场需求、监管路径及国际合作模式的研究，为未来产品进入国际市场奠定基础并及早思考产品出海计划。



值得一提的是，除了脑机接口，我国近来在医疗器械标准话语权上正奋起直追。


根据近日国家标准委的披露，今年以来，我国提出的7项医疗器械领域国际标准提案获ISO批准立项，创历史同期新高。截至目前，我国已牵头制定25项医疗器械领域国际标准，涵盖人工智能医疗器械、心血管植入物、组织工程医疗器械、基因测序等。其中，11项已发布、14项正有序推进。


在医疗器械标准上，中国曾长期是追赶者，出海要按别人的规则办事。脑机接口是全球尚未定型的战略赛道。基于过往的长期积累，我国第一次有机会先走一步。也希望我国书写的脑机接口标准，真正成为我国冲击脑机接口领跑的序幕。

title: What a stranded scooter taught a future physician [PODCAST]
summary: Listen and followApple PodcastsSpotifyYouTubeMore apps · Browse all episodes When an ambulance took a homeless patient to the hospital, his scooter was left behind on the street. It meant everything t...
full_content:
Listen and followApple PodcastsSpotifyYouTubeMore apps · Browse all episodes

When an ambulance took a homeless patient to the hospital, his scooter was left behind on the street. It meant everything to him. Alexander Aschinberg is a premedical student at Northeastern University. This episode is based on his article “Patients experiencing homelessness need more than a cure,” published on KevinMD. You will hear how a summer as a volunteer at Lawndale Christian Health Center in Chicago took him into homeless shelters with a mobile care team. He describes finding the scooter, returning it, and then moving it again when the hospital discharged the patient to a day shelter and could not transport it. You will hear what he saw inside the shelters, from crowded cots and little privacy to staff struggling to keep them clean. He also explains how the physicians and care managers there, some of whom had known patients for 20 years, helped them with housing, Medicaid, and rides to appointments. Press play to hear the kind of doctor this summer made him want to become.

If this episode helped, follow The Podcast by KevinMD on Apple Podcasts or Spotify, and leave a rating.

Partner with me on the KevinMD platform. With more than 100 million impressions a year and nearly 750,000 followers, subscribers and email recipients across my channels, I give you direct access to the doctors and patients who matter most. Whether you need a sponsored article, email campaign, video interview, or a spot right here on the podcast, I offer the trusted space your brand deserves to be heard. Let’s work together to tell your story.

PARTNER WITH KEVINMD → https://kevinmd.com/influencer

SUBSCRIBE TO THE PODCAST → https://www.kevinmd.com/podcast

Transcript

Kevin Pho: Hi, and welcome to the show. Subscribe at KevinMD.com/podcast. Today, we welcome Alexander Aschinberg. He’s a premedical student. Today’s KevinMD article is “Patients experiencing homelessness need more than a cure.” Alex, welcome to the show.

Alexander Aschinberg: Thank you. It’s an honor to be here. I’m really excited to be on the podcast, and thanks for having me.

Kevin Pho: All right. So let’s start by briefly sharing your story, and then tell us what made you share your story on KevinMD in the first place.

Alexander Aschinberg: Yes. I’m a fourth-year mechanical engineering and history major at Northeastern University who’s also on a pre-med track. I’m a Chicago native, born and raised in the west suburbs, and I’m the co-founder and president of the Salud Más Allá Health Care Initiative. The article I wrote was about an experience I had this summer while I was a summer volunteer at Lawndale Christian Health Center, and an experience I had with a patient and his health care needs.

I started writing this article as a draft of a personal statement. As a pre-med student, you spend a lot of time thinking about why you want to become a doctor and the reason you want to become a doctor. For me, what really solidified that was my experience with Lawndale Christian Health Center this summer, and especially this experience with Mr. Simmons. But the more I wrote this article, the more I realized I had a lot more to say than the 5,300-character limit they give you for a personal statement. So from there, I decided to write out everything I wanted to say and see where it went, and I ended up going a lot over that limit.

But I think it worked out really well, because I was able to tie in bigger themes like the death disparity gap in Chicago. That’s something they talked about a lot at Lawndale. And I was able to turn it into a pretty good editorial, or at least an editorial I was proud of. So it was something I wanted to get out there, and I wanted to be able to get my story published. I definitely think it still reads a bit like a personal statement, but I think that’s one of its strong suits.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

Kevin Pho: All right. So for those who didn’t get a chance to read your story, tell us about your experience at Lawndale Christian Health Center, and tell us why this particular patient had such an impact on you.

Alexander Aschinberg: I had a very diverse role at Lawndale Christian Health Center. They didn’t have a summer volunteer program in place before me, so they made an exception for me, and I guess I was paving the way for what summer volunteers would be in the future. So I was able to help out, shadow, and participate in a lot of different programs they had, whether that was administrative work or work with the mobile care team.

Part of being on the mobile care team was that they would have clinics set up at different shelters throughout the week, and I was able to visit a lot of the shelters that Lawndale provided health care for in Chicago and see what that process was like. It was really eye-opening, because I’d never been to a homeless shelter before. Just being able to see what that was like, and the whole experience of being in the shelter, was definitely eye-opening.

But the experience I wrote about with Mr. Simmons was particularly special, because it was one I was able to see through from, I guess, beginning to end. For those who haven’t read the article, Mr. Simmons is a beloved patient of the Lawndale Mobile Care Team. He’s always been super nice, super caring, and friendly with the whole care team. He would drive around on his patented blue scooter. One day, really early in my volunteering, I think the first week, we got a call that Mr. Simmons had been taken to the hospital the night before, and his scooter was left behind where the ambulance picked him up. He was in distress, because the scooter meant everything to him. He used it to get everywhere. It was his primary means of transportation.

So we went out trying to find his scooter. We knew the street it was on, but that was about it, so it could have been anywhere on the street. It could have been moved, but the fact that it survived the night just lying out there on the street was a miracle in itself. We were able to get the scooter and drop it off to him in the hospital, and he was delighted. It was an amazing experience being able to drop that off and return it to him. It meant the world to him.

So that’s where we thought the story would end, on a high note. But a couple of days later, we got a call from the hospital saying that he was being discharged, and that not only was he being sent back to the day shelter where he was picked up, but they also couldn’t transport his scooter. So from there, we had to go back to the hospital, pick up his scooter, and drop it off back where we had returned it. That whole cycle, that whole process of being able to do something good and then seeing that progress taken back, really had an impact on me.

It really gave me an insight into the health care system that I didn’t get from just shadowing doctors or being an MA or any prior health care experience. It was a really real view of what it was like for patients: the economic disparities, how patients are treated, and the everyday life these patients have to go through. That’s really what motivated me to write about this particular experience. But my whole time at Lawndale was an amazing experience, and I had so many opportunities to shadow amazing physicians, meet amazing people, and learn about the city of Chicago in a way I’d never seen before.

Kevin Pho: So you said that this whole experience, working in a homeless shelter, seeing the neighborhoods you drove through, and what happened to Mr. Simmons after he was discharged from the hospital, was eye-opening. You used that word. So tell us about some specific things that really resonated with you and really taught you something you didn’t know or see before.

Alexander Aschinberg: As I said earlier, I consider myself a Chicago native. I know some people who live downtown wouldn’t consider the west suburbs quite Chicago. But I’ve lived here my whole life, and I grew up going downtown in Chicago every weekend. So before this experience, I thought I knew the city pretty well. But going to Lawndale and getting thrown into it, I really got to see places in the city I’d never experienced before. I went to neighborhoods I’d never been to and shelters I didn’t know existed. So it really opened my eyes to how little I knew about what it’s really like for different people to live in Chicago, and what the city is like as a whole.

On the way to and from the shelters, I was able to see the neighborhoods and see signs of neighborhoods that used to be prospering. You would see beautiful architectural buildings that were completely in ruins and abandoned. You’d see signs for restaurants, some of which looked delicious, but they would all be closed down. They looked like they hadn’t been operating for fifty years. So really seeing the deterioration of some of the communities you would pass, and also seeing the shelters themselves and how people live their everyday lives so differently from what you would expect, was really eye-opening.

Kevin Pho: So describe what it’s like inside a shelter for those who may not be familiar with that. Like you said, this was maybe the first time you went into a shelter. So what was it like? And tell us about some of the things that would be an impediment to the residents’ health, based on how they lived in a shelter.

Alexander Aschinberg: One of the main things that surprised me was how different shelters were. Going into it, I thought all shelters were the same. I thought it was just bunk beds or cots all lined up next to each other. But there was really a big diversity between different types of shelters.

One of the main shelters we went to is SPARC, the Shelter Placement and Resource Center. That’s where people go to get placed into different shelters, so it was a very short-term shelter, because people would get placed out. It was in a warehouse. There were no windows, and it was very confined. There would be a women’s and a men’s lounge section where they would be during the day, maybe with a movie playing and just folding chairs. Then they would have a sleeping section with just cots lined up next to each other.

But then you would go to different shelters, and it was a completely different layout. At the other one, Harrison, which I guess we call Harrison Shelter because it’s on that street, but which is run by Franciscan Outreach, there were no day rooms. It was all bunk beds. And then we would go to other shelters that were completely different. They’d have purpose-built clinics inside the shelter, and it would look like a school, with a cafeteria, nice lighting, and everything perfectly clean. And some shelters were dirty. So there was a big variety between the shelters, in their standards and the living conditions within them.

As far as how it can be an impediment to getting proper health care, one of the main things was privacy, because some of these shelters would be completely open, and you never got a moment away from other people. Your whole life is concerned with whether people are trying to steal your stuff, and whether you are going to be safe spending the night there, because fights would break out occasionally, or people would steal belongings if they were just left on the cot or left out in the open. So I think that was a main one.

I would say the cleanliness was another impediment. The shelter staff always tried to do an amazing job. They would always be cleaning up messes that occurred. They would always be mopping and cleaning the floors. But there’s only so much you can do when you have so many people crammed in. At SPARC, they actually recently had to lower the number of people they were able to take in. They went from four hundred and cut it all the way down to two hundred, because the size made it too difficult to keep up that standard. I definitely think those were the two things I saw that most affected their ability to get the proper health standard.

Kevin Pho: So one of the things about your experience, as you describe it, is that you were able to see things outside of the exam room, so you were able to get a full picture of how a patient’s social determinants of health affected them in the exam room when they got to the clinic. So what would be an example of what a physician would see in the exam room about how a patient’s social determinants of health would affect their medical treatment when they come to the clinic?

Alexander Aschinberg: That’s a great question. One of the things at Lawndale that really stood out to me as well was how the physicians really took care of the whole patient instead of just their medical needs. The relationship I saw between the physicians and their patients was like none other I’d seen while shadowing or working in health care facilities, because they had an extremely close bond.

A lot of the patients in the shelters don’t have very many friends or people they can confide in, tell stories to, or have a personal relationship with, but that’s really what the physicians became at Lawndale. They became more than a physician, more like a friend or a family member. A lot of the patient meetings turned away from just talking about their health care needs and their medicine and more toward how they were doing personally, the experiences they had seen in the shelters, how they were trying to get better housing, or how they were applying for Medicaid and getting the resources they needed.

That was something that really stuck out to me: how far beyond health care they went, and how close-knit they were with their patients and the community. Some of the providers had known some of their patients for twenty years. So they really were able to get close with them and confide in them in a way I hadn’t seen anywhere else. Above that, they worked really closely with the care managers, who were able to get patients transportation to the appointments they needed, get them into some of the wider Lawndale programs, and make sure they could get all the resources and knew the resources that were available to them.

Kevin Pho: So this whole experience obviously made an impact on you. How do you think it will influence you as a future physician?

Alexander Aschinberg: I hope to be what I’ll call a Lawndale physician. I hope to be a physician who looks beyond just the medical needs of a person, looks more into their holistic needs, and is able to have that close relationship with them. I hope I have such a good relationship with my patients that they consider me a friend and a family member and someone they can confide in, not just someone they come to with a problem, hoping to get it fixed. So as far as the type of physician I want to be, that’s the standard I hope I can hold myself to.

Kevin Pho: We’re talking to Alex Aschinberg. He’s a premedical student. Today’s KevinMD article is “Patients experiencing homelessness need more than a cure.” Alex, let’s end with your take-home messages to the KevinMD audience.

Alexander Aschinberg: While I have this platform, I really want to thank my parents. They’ve been super supportive of my whole pre-med journey, and really my whole life, pushing me to pursue what I’m passionate about. They’ve been a huge motivator and a huge influence, especially my mom as well. Based on my experience at Lawndale, we started a health care initiative called Salud Más Allá, which means “health care beyond” in Spanish, aimed at supporting local and international health care institutions. A lot of my experiences at Lawndale have really shaped the impact I was able to have and my goals with that, and she’s been a huge factor in that. I wouldn’t have been able to expand it to what it’s become, or get the outreach we’ve been able to get, without her. So I really wanted to thank my parents for all their support.

Kevin Pho: Alex, thank you so much for sharing your story, time, and insight. Thanks again for coming on the show.

Alexander Aschinberg: Thank you. I really appreciate you giving me the opportunity to be here, and this was a really great experience. Thank you.

title: GLP-1 mental health needs a plan, not just a prescription
summary: Picture a woman at her kitchen table at 2 a.m. The scale has moved. Her clothes fit differently. Everyone tells her she looks wonderful. She feels flat, frightened, or oddly grieving, and has no idea ...
full_content:
Picture a woman at her kitchen table at 2 a.m. The scale has moved. Her clothes fit differently. Everyone tells her she looks wonderful. She feels flat, frightened, or oddly grieving, and has no idea whom she could tell.

Now picture a man whose blood sugar has finally come down. His doctor is pleased. He has been called a success. He has not felt like himself for weeks, and nobody has asked.

Nursing teaches you that what people say first is rarely all of it. I have spent more than thirty years as a nurse. I am also someone who has struggled while taking a glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) medicine.

I started without doing what I would do for anyone else. I did not research it. Since then, I have learned that knowing what to do and being able to do it for yourself are different things.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

I have prediabetes, and five members of my family developed type 2 diabetes in later life. I understand why people want these medicines. I understand why they fear losing access.

I had low moods, anxiety, frustration, and moments of hopelessness while managing symptoms that kept changing. Gastric trouble made eating difficult. I felt lethargic and foggy. People told me to “just eat.” I wanted one normal meal without gastric upset. Just one thing I could eat comfortably.

My head had not caught up with what my eyes were seeing in the mirror. I did not recognize the woman looking back. I wondered what was happening to my relationship with food. I could not work it out alone.

Was my difficulty eating something I should discuss with an eating disorder specialist? I needed someone qualified to explore that with me.

Other users have spoken to me about anxiety, depression, and low mood. Some describe eating habits that worry them and wonder whether they are moving toward an eating disorder. They need assessment, including attention to physical symptoms and nutrition, and room to explain what has changed.

My daughter has anxiety. As her mother, I care deeply about what happens after someone asks for help. I want support to be available while they still have the courage and energy to seek it.

The research offers reassurance. In January 2026, the Food and Drug Administration reported a review of 91 placebo-controlled trials involving 107,910 people. It found no increased risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior, depression, or anxiety, and requested removal of the suicidality warning from affected U.S. labels.

That finding deserves to be heard. So do patients describing distress. My experience cannot establish what caused it. Symptoms, difficulty eating, changes in my body, and fear about treatment were happening together.

A 2026 JAMA Network Open interview study of 30 adults across 15 U.S. states described reduced food noise alongside adverse effects, stigma, and uneven clinical support. These interviews illuminate experiences; they cannot tell us how common those experiences are or establish medication causation.

I want us to ask what food meant to someone before treatment. If it offered comfort during anxiety, what helps them cope now? If they feel grief or uncertainty about a changing body, can they say so without feeling ungrateful? Those questions give a clinician somewhere to begin, without assuming a diagnosis or deciding in advance that the medicine must be responsible.

The scale of use makes this urgent. In November 2025, KFF reported that 18 percent of U.S. adults had used a GLP-1 medicine and 12 percent were currently using one. A 2024 Oxford Economics forecast projected around 40 million Americans using these medicines by 2030. That is a forecast, dependent on access and uptake, and says nothing about how many will experience psychological distress.

I read that figure and think about the person who cannot bring themselves to say they are struggling. Who will notice? Who will help if the referral is unaffordable?

Some support exists. Australia’s Better Access initiative provides mental health treatment rebates for eligible people. In the United States, the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge is widening medication access for eligible beneficiaries. As access expands, service planners should explain how patients will reach psychological care when needed.

I want mood, sleep, eating, and coping discussed before treatment and revisited during follow-up, including treatment changes and stopping. Appropriate screening should lead to clinical assessment and a clear plan. Online prescribing should carry the same expectation of accessible follow-up as an appointment in a consulting room.

For governments, insurers, and health departments, the questions are practical. Who funds the time to ask? Who pays when assessment identifies someone needing help? Can practices reach psychologists, dietitians, and eating disorder specialists? How long will patients wait, and who checks whether they receive care?

Fund clinician training, coordinated referrals, and affordable remote care where appropriate. Measure whether people reach support. A referral letter alone cannot tell us that.

Peer groups can offer companionship and language for experiences people struggle to explain. Administrators need training, current referral information, and a clear response to concerning posts. Members need to know when a group is monitored and where to seek urgent help directly.

At the next appointment, I would ask three questions.

  • How are you feeling in yourself, including your mood and enjoyment of ordinary life?
  • Has eating become difficult, frightening, or hard to manage?
  • What support do you need, and how will we make sure you can reach it?

Silence is not safety. The evidence is reassuring about psychiatric risk overall. It cannot tell us everything about how an individual is coping. Whatever medicine someone takes, they deserve to be asked how they are and to know where to go if the answer is “not well.”

At follow-up, I would ask clinicians to make room for the part of the story a patient may struggle to tell. Ask about eating comfortably, managing work, and enjoying ordinary life. Explore physical symptoms, nutrition, and emotional distress together, including fears about continuing or stopping treatment.

Before the appointment ends, agree on the next step. Arrange further assessment or referral when needed, explain whom to contact if things worsen, and set a date to check back. I needed help making sense of what was happening to me. Follow-up should make that help easier to reach.

Patience C. Ennis is a registered nurse, author, Results Coach, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) user, and the founder of Body Compass, an education and navigation platform for people living with, considering, or moving beyond GLP-1 treatment. A graduate of King’s College London, she draws on more than three decades of clinical experience across emergency, community, palliative, and aged care, bringing together clinical knowledge, lived experience, and patient education to address the questions that often sit beyond the prescription.

Through Body Compass, she develops evidence-informed resources, books, practical tools, news updates, and non-clinical coaching support designed to help people understand changing appetite, side effects, strength, food noise, treatment adaptation, maintenance, and stopping. Her work is grounded in clarity, dignity, and honest interpretation of evidence, without hype, shame, or false certainty. Her aim is not to tell people what to decide, but to help them understand the terrain, ask better questions, and navigate metabolic health with greater confidence in everyday life and care.

She is the author of When GLP-1 Feels Different: Plateau, Food Noise, Adaptation and the Fear of “Resistance” (2026), available on Amazon and through Body Compass. Her other titles include Living Well on GLP-1 Medication: A Practical Guide to Everyday Life Beyond the Prescription, The Body Compass 30-Day Navigation Diary: A Reflective Daily Companion for GLP-1 Treatment, and The 30-Day GLP-1 Navigation Companion: Observation, Reflection, Preparation, Navigation.

She shares updates on LinkedIn, Facebook, the Body Compass Facebook page, Instagram, X, TikTok, and YouTube.

title: Why pain management education in medical school falls short
summary: As a prominent health care educator and patient advocate, I receive multiple pleas every month for help locating a doctor who is still accepting patients for pain care in the currently very hostile U....
full_content:
As a prominent health care educator and patient advocate, I receive multiple pleas every month for help locating a doctor who is still accepting patients for pain care in the currently very hostile U.S. and Canadian regulatory environment. Many clinicians have left the field entirely, rather than put themselves at risk for enforcement raids on their offices, with records seized and staff and patients intimidated. And make no mistake: This description is by no means overly dramatic. I have heard similar words from multiple clinicians who have been subjected to such raids.

I personally make a practice of distributing such requests for referral to a private network of clinicians who are knowledgeable in several specialties helpful in pain management. In response to one such recent inquiry, I received an unexpectedly candid, wide-ranging, and authoritative response from Ellen N. Thompson, MBBS, FRCPC, which I incorporate below with minor editing for clarity to U.S. readers.

For those unfamiliar with Canadian education, MBBS is a Bachelor of Medicine, Bachelor of Surgery degree, roughly equivalent to an MD. FRCPC translates as “Fellow of the Royal College of Physicians of Canada (Division of Medicine).” This is a post-nominal designation (not an academic degree) awarded to certified medical specialists in Canada. It has similarities to our board certification process.

The following narrative is that of Dr. Thompson, used and attributed by name with her permission.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

“I’m sorry to be unable to help this lady. She is too far away, and at age 83 I am retired. After a long career in anesthesiology and pain medicine, I am distraught at the lack of progress in pain medicine. If anything, pain medicine has regressed.

“It is true that 50+ years ago we were taught very little of any value, even at Newcastle upon Tyne, England, in 1970, one of the top two medical schools in England (Birmingham was the other). I then spent four years in an anesthesiology fellowship. On entering general practice, the lack of teaching even in that fellowship became readily apparent. Fortunately, I personally had the genes predisposing one to musculoskeletal pain. So telling patients that their complaints were imaginary or psychological was not an option for me.

“I often mention that it was the pain patients who drove me out of general practice; they made me feel incompetent or inadequate.

“I soon joined the International Association for the Study of Pain and its Canadian national subsidiaries. I attended congresses. Pat Wall, Ron Melzack, and other world leaders became friends and mentors. I lectured to medical students to pass on what I learned. But note: In the 1970s, Ottawa medical students only received two lectures (75 minutes of formal teaching) in the second of four years during the early years of this century. This was more than some Canadian medical schools, some of which still had no formal teaching. Veterinary students received more instruction about managing pain in their clients.

“Disability due to musculoskeletal pain costs western societies as much or more than heart disease. Why then, this disparity in teaching students and trainees?

“Then came the opioid epidemic and the horrific mismanagement by powerful individuals who did not know (or care) what they did not know. Pain patients, who had had a reasonable quality of life with sensible/effective doses of opioids, had these taken away. Patients are still suffering, even as we know fentanyl powder brought in from India or China and made to look like OxyContin tabs was the real problem.

“How many generations will continue this needless suffering? When will some of the knowledge we have possessed since the days of Wall and Melzack be transferred? And from my own life, the knowledge of Janet Travell and David Simons about optimal management of myofascial pain, the most common and most readily treated form of pain.

“It seems that Travell and Simons’ treatment was far too simple, too cheap, and too effective. Big back operations repeated multiple times provided far greater incomes in the American ‘for profit’ system.

“Complex regional pain syndrome (reflex sympathetic dystrophy) could also be cured if the correct diagnosis was made in time, and simple local anesthetic blocks correctly administered. To do this, adequate teaching must be provided.”

Thank you, Dr. Thompson. The issues outlined above are measurably worse today than during Dr. Thompson’s clinical education over 50 years ago. This is true with regard to both clinical education and public health policy enforced by U.S. public health and law enforcement agencies.

As acknowledged by Nora Volkow, MD (director of the U.S. National Institute on Drug Abuse), veterinarians still receive more education in pain management than MD candidates in medical schools. A 2011 study in The Journal of Pain found that U.S. medical schools allotted a median of just 9 hours to pain education across the entire curriculum.

Pain is the number one reason why people contact a doctor. According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), about 17 million U.S. adults suffer from “high-impact” chronic pain, and about 51.6 million from chronic pain overall. Other sources such as the Cleveland Clinic estimate the number of chronic sufferers at 50 million overall.

Contrast these numbers against the numbers of doctors being trained: Between 330 and 400 doctors are trained in specialized pain management fellowships each year in the United States. About 7,350 physicians now practice primarily in pain management overall, for a patient population of at least 20 million. Many of both have completed residencies in other specialties, notably anesthesiology, internal medicine, or emergency medicine.

There is wide consensus among clinical professionals and patients that this mismatch between patients in pain and clinicians who will treat them is a direct consequence of the hostile U.S. and Canadian regulatory environment. That environment is largely created by weaponization of U.S. public health agency clinical guidelines on opioid prescribing. Despite professional groups pointing out the need for individualized patient care based on clinical judgment rather than arbitrary dose levels, doctors continue to face state laws implementing limits on morphine milligram equivalent dose. Even when exceptions are identified in such laws, the administrative burden that they impose is a highly effective deterrent from treating patients as individuals.

So what’s to be done? In the author’s opinion and those of millions of pain patients, if the CDC, the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the Drug Enforcement Administration are ever to be taken seriously again, these agencies must outright withdraw and repudiate existing, fatally flawed opioid prescribing guidelines and related FDA risk evaluation and mitigation strategies. Then the agencies need to advise all U.S. state boards and law enforcement authorities to do the same.

As we have seen from altogether too many current examples, political influence in all of its forms is absolute poison to good medical practice and evidence-based patient welfare.

Richard A. Lawhern is a nationally recognized health care educator and patient advocate who has spent three decades researching pain management and addiction policy. His extensive body of work, including over 300 published papers and interviews, reflects a deep critique of U.S. health care agencies and their approaches to chronic pain treatment. Now retired from formal academic affiliations, Richard continues to engage with professional and public audiences through platforms such as The National Campaign to Protect People in Pain, LinkedIn, Facebook, and his contributions to KevinMD. His advocacy extends to online communities like Protect People in Pain, where he works to elevate the voices of patients navigating restrictive opioid policies. Among his many publications is a guideline on opioid use for chronic non-cancer pain, reflecting his commitment to evidence-based reform in pain medicine. He was recognized in Marquis Who’s Who in 2025 and named a Fellow of the European Society of Medicine in 2026.

title: Psychiatric discharge planning must cover the first week
summary: When an adult leaves a psychiatric hospital stay, the discharge paperwork usually says the same thing: Follow up with outpatient care. On paper, the plan is complete. In real life, the week that follo...
full_content:
When an adult leaves a psychiatric hospital stay, the discharge paperwork usually says the same thing: Follow up with outpatient care. On paper, the plan is complete. In real life, the week that follows is often the hardest one.

As a counselor, I work with adults in the weeks after a hospital stay. What I have learned is that the gap is rarely about motivation. It is about structure. In the hospital, the day has a shape: groups in the morning, check-ins, meals at set times, people who notice. Then someone goes home to an empty apartment and a first therapy appointment that may be two or three weeks away. Weekly therapy is a great fit for a lot of people. For someone a few days out of the hospital, an hour a week can feel like being dropped from a height. Here is what I wish every referring clinician knew about that week:

  • The level of care should step down, not fall off: Between a hospital stay and weekly therapy, there is a middle level: intensive outpatient care, several sessions a week, often in groups, while the person sleeps at home and starts to rebuild a routine. It is not a lesser version of the hospital. It is a bridge with its own purpose: practicing skills in real life and coming back to talk about how it went.
  • Groups do something individual sessions cannot: People arrive expecting to sit quietly through an hour. They often leave having heard their own thoughts in someone else’s words. For adults coming out of a hospital stay, that is often the first week they stop feeling like the only one.
  • Timing matters more than the perfect program: A good program that starts in three days beats an ideal program that starts in a month. When you write the discharge plan, ask how fast the next level of care can actually begin, and whether it fits around the person’s work and family.
  • Measure, and keep measuring: Standard questionnaires like the PHQ-9 and GAD-7, repeated on a schedule, tell the team and the client whether things are moving. They are not a replacement for clinical judgment. They are a shared language for a conversation that is otherwise easy to avoid.
  • Keep the referring clinician in the loop: With the client’s permission, the therapist or psychiatrist who referred someone should hear how they are doing. When the person steps back down to weekly therapy, nobody should be starting from scratch.

None of this is complicated. Most of it is just structure, delivered at the right moment. The week after the hospital is when that structure matters most, and it is the week our system is most likely to leave empty.

If you or someone you know is struggling, call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

Anna Green is a mental health counselor.

title: Should doctors prescribe Cialis for longevity? Not yet
summary: Apparently, we’ve discovered another longevity miracle. This time it’s Cialis. A recent Verywell Health article reports that men taking tadalafil, the popular erectile dysfunction drug, ha...
full_content:
Apparently, we’ve discovered another longevity miracle. This time it’s Cialis.

A recent Verywell Health article reports that men taking tadalafil, the popular erectile dysfunction drug, have a 34 percent lower risk of death, a 27 percent lower risk of heart attack, a 34 percent lower risk of stroke, and a 32 percent lower risk of dementia. Impressive numbers. One might reasonably wonder why we’re not putting it in the drinking water.

There’s just one problem. No randomized trial has demonstrated that tadalafil prevents heart attacks, dementia, or death in otherwise healthy men taking it for longevity. And that distinction matters.

The problem with the magic numbers

The figures come from a study published in the American Journal of Medicine involving more than 500,000 men with erectile dysfunction. Researchers examined electronic health records and found that men prescribed tadalafil experienced fewer adverse cardiovascular events and deaths over three years.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

But the men weren’t randomly assigned to tadalafil or placebo. Researchers compared patients who received prescriptions with those who didn’t. That’s not a minor statistical technicality. It’s the difference between discovering that a medication works and discovering that people who take it are different from people who don’t.

Consider two sixty-five-year-old men with erectile dysfunction. One exercises regularly, sees his physician, remains sexually active, and feels well enough to seek treatment. The other has significant coronary disease, limited exercise tolerance, and takes nitrates for angina.

Guess which one is more likely to receive Cialis? And which one is more likely to be alive three years later?

The investigators used propensity-score matching to adjust for measured differences between patients. That’s helpful, but it cannot account for everything: physical fitness, frailty, sexual activity, health-seeking behavior, or the severity of underlying illness.

There’s another problem. Patients taking nitrates generally cannot receive tadalafil because the combination can cause dangerous hypotension. Some patients with substantial cardiovascular disease are therefore systematically less likely to receive the drug. Epidemiologists call this confounding by contraindication.

I call it a pretty good reason to be skeptical.

Where’s the absolute risk reduction?

We’re told the relative risk of death was 34 percent lower. But what does that mean for an individual patient? What were the actual event rates? What’s the absolute difference? And, most importantly, how much of that difference was caused by tadalafil?

The article doesn’t adequately answer these questions. Even if we knew the absolute difference between the groups, we couldn’t legitimately calculate a treatment number needed to treat (NNT) without establishing causality.

I’ve spent much of my career watching relative risk reductions presented as though they tell us everything we need to know about a drug. They don’t.

A 34 percent relative reduction might represent an enormous clinical benefit or a relatively small absolute difference. And in an observational study, it might not represent a drug benefit at all.

The dementia studies that complicate the story

The reported 32 percent reduction in dementia is particularly appealing. Who wouldn’t want a pill that improves erections and protects the brain? Unfortunately, other studies tell a less exciting story.

A study published online in 2024 in Neuroepidemiology compared 5,204 men starting daily low-dose tadalafil for benign prostatic hyperplasia with 18,565 men starting alpha-blockers. The result? Essentially no difference in dementia risk. Hazard ratio: 0.99 (95 percent confidence interval 0.88 to 1.12).

The same investigators examined another cohort of 133,336 men with erectile dysfunction. Again, no statistically significant protection: hazard ratio 0.95 (95 percent confidence interval 0.86 to 1.04).

A separate Medicare-based study published in Brain Communications in 2022 also failed to find convincing evidence that phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE5) inhibitors reduced Alzheimer’s disease or related dementia.

To be fair, not every study has been negative. A large 2024 study in Neurology reported an 18 percent lower risk of Alzheimer’s disease among men prescribed PDE5 inhibitors. But when investigators excluded the first three years of follow-up, the association weakened and was no longer statistically significant. That should make us wonder whether we’re observing a drug effect or simply identifying men who were healthier before they ever swallowed their first pill.

A 2025 Mendelian randomization study also found no evidence supporting a causal protective effect against Alzheimer’s disease, although that method has limitations of its own. The Verywell article acknowledges observational bias, to its credit. But the conflicting evidence deserves more attention than it receives.

A beautiful mechanism proves very little

Tadalafil inhibits phosphodiesterase-5, increasing cGMP signaling and promoting vascular relaxation. Researchers have proposed benefits involving endothelial function, blood flow, platelet activity, and oxidative stress.

All interesting. All biologically plausible. And none establishes that tadalafil extends life.

I’ve practiced medicine long enough to watch plenty of beautiful mechanisms collapse when someone finally conducts a randomized trial. Improving blood flow isn’t necessarily the same as preventing a heart attack. Improving a laboratory measurement isn’t necessarily the same as preventing a stroke.

A drug’s mechanism tells us why it might work. It doesn’t tell us whether it does.

But what about the cardiovascular studies?

A 2024 study in Clinical Cardiology reported 44 percent lower all-cause mortality among men exposed to tadalafil. Again, impressive.

But this was another observational analysis. Men with tadalafil prescription claims were compared with men without PDE5 inhibitor claims. Differences in baseline health, treatment selection, and exposure classification remain important concerns.

Interestingly, among men with established coronary artery disease, the mortality association wasn’t statistically significant. The hazard ratio was 1.40, although the confidence interval was wide (0.57 to 3.42), making the result inconclusive. That doesn’t demonstrate harm. It simply doesn’t establish protection.

A 2024 meta-analysis pooled sixteen studies and found associations between PDE5 inhibitor use and lower cardiovascular event rates and mortality. But fifteen of those studies were observational.

Pooling studies doesn’t eliminate the biases they share. Sometimes it just gives us a more precise estimate of the wrong answer.

So should we prescribe Cialis for longevity?

Not yet.

Tadalafil is an effective treatment for erectile dysfunction and urinary symptoms associated with benign prostatic hyperplasia. It also has an established role in pulmonary arterial hypertension. Those are legitimate reasons to prescribe it. Extending lifespan in otherwise healthy people is not an established indication.

The drug isn’t harmless. It can cause headache, flushing, back pain, hypotension, and potentially serious interactions with nitrates. Rare cases of sudden visual or hearing loss have also been reported, although causality remains uncertain.

When a medication treats a bothersome symptom, accepting some risk may be reasonable. When we’re treating healthy people for a benefit that hasn’t been demonstrated, the calculation changes.

I would love for tadalafil to prevent cardiovascular disease and dementia. It’s inexpensive, familiar, and physiologically interesting. The observational findings are worth investigating.

Unfortunately, large randomized outcomes trials are expensive, and generic drugs rarely attract enthusiastic commercial sponsors. But that doesn’t lower the standard of evidence.

The lesson we’re missing

There’s one genuinely important cardiovascular message buried in this story. Erectile dysfunction can be an early marker of vascular disease.

A middle-aged man presenting with new erectile dysfunction deserves a cardiovascular risk assessment, including blood pressure, lipids, glucose, smoking history, and an honest discussion about his vascular health. That may prove considerably more valuable than handing him a prescription and suggesting it will protect his arteries.

If tadalafil improves his sexual function, wonderful. That’s a meaningful benefit in its own right.

But let’s stop confusing an association with a demonstrated treatment effect. We’ve spent decades allowing relative risk reductions to substitute for absolute benefits. Now we’re increasingly allowing observational correlations to substitute for randomized evidence.

Perhaps tadalafil really does extend life. I hope it does. But hope isn’t evidence, and a statistically significant association isn’t a clinical trial.

Cialis may help men get more out of life. Whether it helps them get more life remains unproven. Until someone demonstrates otherwise, that’s the distinction worth keeping erect.

Larry Kaskel is an internist and self-described “lipidologist in recovery” who has practiced medicine for more than 35 years, with an emphasis on prevention, wellness, and longevity. He runs a concierge medical practice in the Chicago area and serves on the teaching faculty at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

He is the former host of Lipid Luminations on ReachMD and author of Dr. Kaskel’s Living in Wellness. His writing frequently challenges conventional medical wisdom and explores new approaches to preventing chronic disease.

Dr. Kaskel is also the founder and CEO of Holy Chiat, a fiber supplement.
