title: AI4S火热，离“ChatGPT时刻”还有多远？
summary:
掌握在企业自己手里。两类条件同时具备的行业很少，目前跑在前面的，往往只占了其中一头。

医药是产业条件最成熟的领域。

新药研发投入高、周期长、失败率高，从药物分子筛选到临床试验，可能需要十余年。如果能缩短早期研发时间、减少无效实验，就有理由尝试
full_content:
一种帮助药物进入细胞的肽分子，从设计到验证过去可能耗上一年，如今在 AI4S 公司被压缩到两三个月：模型负责设计筛选，自动化平台接手实验。融资热度随之升温，但让 AI 从提效走到被产业认可的成果，中间仍有不短的距离。

一种帮助药物进入细胞的肽分子，从开始设计到进入实验验证，要花多长时间？

过去，仅仅是从海量候选分子里筛出有希望的那几个，就可能耗上一年甚至更久。而在AI4S创业公司智源深澜，这件事被压缩到了两三个月：AI模型负责设计和筛选，自动化实验平台接手后续实验，原本要靠科研人员一轮轮试错的工作，交给了算法和机器。

类似的变化正在更多实验室发生。查文献、分析数据、设计分子、规划实验，AI正在介入过去高度依赖科学家知识和经验的环节。一些创业者的目标更远——让AI独立提出科学问题、发现新知识。

这一方向被称为AI for Science（AI4S，人工智能驱动科学研究）。

今年以来，这条赛道的融资热度明显提升。据媒体报道，今年前10个月，国内AI4S赛道发生超过80笔融资，已披露融资总额超过200亿元。科理新序、元材新界等成立不久的创业公司接连获得融资，资本正加速涌入生命科学、材料研发等方向。AI4S创业公司深度原理则推出科研大模型Hydrogen-1.0，尝试让AI参与实验设计和新材料发现。

大厂也在加速布局。11月16日，阿里发布的Qwen4-Max展示了自主设计新型冷却液分子，并调用自动化实验平台完成合成与测试的能力。此前，Anthropic的Claude Fable 5.2和Mythos 5.2、腾讯的混元Hy4正式版也相继展示了通用大模型解决理论物理、数学研究等领域复杂问题的能力。

科研一直被视为最依赖人类判断的领域之一。一个假设成不成立，要靠真实实验检验；一项发现有没有价值，要靠科学家判断。那么，AI究竟能替科学家做多少事？它离独立完成科学发现还有多远？这门生意，又能做多大？

01 科学家开始培养自己的“接班人”

智源深澜创始人王承志至今记得读博时的一段经历。

为了找到一种能发酵特定化合物的肠道菌，他先把约一万株菌混在一起发酵，确认目标菌就在其中后，再用二分法不断缩小范围筛选，前后花了大半年。

他一度怀疑，自己千辛万苦考上北大，为什么做的是这些重复工作？后来出国交流，他发现哈佛、耶鲁的一些研究人员也在做同样的事。

这不是一个人的困境。科研中，大量时间消耗在重复劳动上，挤占了科学家判断和创造的时间。2024年，王承志创办智源深澜，将AI模型与自动化实验平台结合，希望有一天，AI能从“实验员”变成“科学家”。

重复劳动之外，科研还有两个老问题：周期太长，门槛太高。

轻远科技（杭州）的创始人赵乘乘此前长期从事材料实验研究。她发现，一个科研项目从提出问题到厘清背后的科学规律，往往需要多年。研究过程中还可能出现多种假设、相互矛盾的实验结果，需要科学家不断分析证据、调整判断，问题越复杂，个人越难梳理清楚。

这促使她转向AI4S。她希望未来AI能够参与提出假设、分析证据、设计实验等过程，让已有研究与新实验持续连接，使每一次探索都成为下一次研究的起点，加快发现科学规律的进程。

高门槛则体现在不同学科之间。

科理新序联创兼COO Erik以一个北京大学植物育种科研团队的合作案例为例。该团队具有深厚的植物科学研究积累，但蛋白质设计涉及另一套专业模型与计算流程。过去，研究人员需要额外学习相关工具，或与计算生物学团队合作。借助科理新序开发的科研智能体，他们可以通过自然语言描述研究目标，由AI协助调用蛋白质设计及分析工具，更便捷地开展跨学科探索。

Erik将这种变化称为“科研平权”。在他看来，AI带来的价值不仅是让原本就擅长计算的科学家更高效，也在于让更多非AI背景的研究人员获得先进的科研计算能力。科理新序智能体的使用者有来自口腔医学、类器官、植物育种等细分方向，过去几乎没有专门的AI工具，AI一旦进入，带来的效率提升和“震撼感”要大得多。

其实，用计算机和机器改造科研，并不是新鲜事。机器学习多年前就进入药物研发、材料计算等领域，但过去的算法往往只能解决某一类问题，机器只能执行固定操作，复杂的研究流程仍然需要人来组织。

在Erik看来，今年的升温来自三股力量的汇合：通用大模型的推理、代码和工具调用能力不断提升，让AI能够理解、并拆解复杂研究任务。蛋白质、分子、细胞等领域的专业模型逐渐成熟，越来越多科学问题有了对应的AI工具。再加上，实验室自动化设备也积累到位，能够执行实验操作，并将结果反馈给AI。

那么，科学家已经能把多少工作交给AI？

王承志把AI参与科研的发展过程大致划分为三个阶段：辅助科研、指导科研和自主科研。

在辅助阶段，AI主要帮助科学家处理信息。王承志早年曾带领团队，利用算法把已发表论文中涉及的基因、疾病、药物和分子等信息，连成一张巨大的知识图谱。

这解决的是科学知识分散的问题。一名科学家可能花多年研究某个基因，发现它与某种疾病有关；另一名科学家研究一种药物，恰好发现它能够作用于这个基因。两项研究之间的关联，单靠人读论文很难发现。知识图谱把这些散落的线索串了起来。

到了指导阶段，AI开始参与研究任务的组织和执行。

打个比方，一名生命科学研究人员想优化某种蛋白质，过去要自己查文献、挑选结构预测模型和分析软件、跑完不同的计算任务，再根据结果不断切换工具。现在，科研智能体可以把这些步骤串起来：研究人员提出目标，AI调用相应的模型和工具，完成部分计算，并根据中间结果安排下一步。Erik形容，AI正越来越像一个“非常强的科研搭档”。这个阶段，研究方向和关键决策，仍要由人把关。

自主阶段则要求AI再向前一步，独立完成科学发现。这一步还没有实现。

王承志用自动驾驶来打比方。现在的AI科研类似于辅助驾驶，能够完成相对固定、标准化的实验流程，但还需要科学家下达指令、检查结果，并在遇到复杂情况时进行干预。而未来的AI应该像一辆能够完全自动驾驶的汽车，可以自主寻找问题、设计实验，并根据结果开展下一轮研究。

在那之前，方向盘还握在科学家手里。

02 AI搞科学，难在哪？

AI为什么还接不过方向盘？如果把科研拆成提出假设、设计方案、实验验证、从结果中学习这几个环节，会发现AI要独立完成整个过程，仍然有几道难关。

科研的起点是提出一个好问题，这恰恰是AI最不擅长的。

王承志认为，AI总结已有知识的能力已经远超人类，但创造新知识的能力还“没及格”。AI本质上是一台概率机器，擅长从海量数据中找出普遍规律，却容易忽略那些偏离规律的细微现象。而科学发现，有时就藏在这些意料之外的结果里。

一次不符合预期的实验结果，可能是误差，也可能是突破某个重大发现的关键节点，分辨两者需要科学家的经验和直觉。

Erik将这种判断力称为“科学品味”。哪些问题值得投入，哪些方向可能带来新的发现，需要科学家判断。在算力和实验资源都有限的情况下，研究一个好问题的价值，远大于研究十个、二十个没有意义的问题。

就算能提出好问题，AI在设计方案时也常常力不从心。

科理新序曾与北京大学一个生命科学课题组合作，尝试利用基于通用大语言模型的科研智能体完成复杂分子对接任务。智能体给出初步结果后，研究人员认为还不够好，要求它继续优化。智能体连续进行了五六轮调整，每一轮都反馈自己完成了哪些改进。等研究人员介入检查时才发现，智能体声称的优化并不算优化，有些甚至变得更差。

在Erik看来，通用大语言模型的科研智能体能够调用工具，并不意味着它真正理解工具处理的科学对象。分子和蛋白质是复杂的三维结构，原子之间的位置、距离和相互作用，都可能影响最终性质。智能体所依赖的通用大语言模型主要依靠自然语言进行推理，当三维信息被转换成文字，再交给专业工具执行时，很多关键信息可能在“翻译”中丢失了。

到了实验验证环节，问题又变成了AI生成速度太快，验证跟不上。

王承志观察到，一些AI制药公司一天就能设计出上万个候选分子，但没有足够的实验能力去验证它们究竟有没有用。

在AI辅助科研的领域，用计算机预测、筛选和设计分子的工作通常被称为“干实验”。但要知道这些分子能否发挥预期作用，还得在实验室进行合成、测试和验证，也就是“湿实验”。两者之间的效率差距，被称为“干湿鸿沟”。

Erik算过一笔账，AI生成1000个候选方案很快，但把1000个方案都验证一遍，很慢、很累，也很花钱。如果模型能够提高判断的准确性，只生成10个方案就找到有效结果，价值会更大。行业需要的不只是更强的生成能力，还要减少无效验证。

让机器人接手实验，是一条路径。目前一些自动化实验室已经能够完成特定流程下的批量实验，但科学研究涉及的设备、试剂和操作条件经常变化，工程师需要提前设置流程、调整参数，遇到异常情况也要人工介入。

王承志认为，下一步是让AI学会自主控制设备。科学家只给出一个实验目标，它能通过视觉、触觉等信息感知环境，像孩子学走路一样，在一次次失败中学会操作仪器。他判断，这方面未来几年可能出现重要突破。

科研循环的最后一环，是从实验结果中学习，这离不开科学数据。

王承志告诉「定焦One」，他曾带领团队清洗一批公开的单细胞测序数据，最后发现约95%的数据不适合直接用于模型训练。这些数据来自不同的科研课题，各实验室采用的实验条件、测量方法和数据标准并不一致。研究人员只关心数据能否支撑自己的结论，并不会考虑数据是否能被AI使用。

“垃圾进，一定垃圾出。”在王承志看来，科学模型需要真实、标准化的数据，最好是不同实验室按照同一流程都能得到一致结果的数据。如果训练材料本身存在问题，再精准的算法也无法保证结果可靠。

Erik则更关注已有科学数据的利用，他认为大量公开论文、专利和科研数据还没有得到充分整理和利用。通过科理新序开发的AI工具给这些数据“降噪和清洗”，将分散的科研信息转化为可用于模型训练和科学分析的结构化数据。相比之下，能够检验AI预测是否正确的实验反馈更加稀缺。

围绕着不同的判断，创业公司从不同方向找切入口。

科理新序从科学基座模型切入，先让AI拥有一个更懂科学的“大脑”。科理新序从预训练阶段开始研发跨模态生命科学基座模型，让AI直接学习和理解不同类型的科学信息，包括蛋白质的结构、DNA和RNA序列等，再利用这些信息进行推理和分析，减少无效计算与实验。

智源深澜则将更多精力放在实验能力上，造更多的“手”。在它的实验室里，AI参与设计方案，自动化设备执行，产生的数据再反馈给模型。王承志介绍，平台一天可以完成约3万次实验，这些数据标准统一，可以直接进入模型迭代。

还有企业从专业计算和仿真切入，减少对实验的依赖。优势星启点科学家基金管理合伙人叶亦天提到，在材料等领域，一些公司利用专业算法模拟材料结构、预测性能，再将这些能力做成模型或软件，提供给产业客户。这类公司不需要自建实验室，也更容易接入企业现有的研发流程。

这些不同的技术路线，都在尝试让AI承担更多科研工作。

03 实验室里，挤进了更多行业

尽管AI离独立做科研还有距离，但在一些行业里，企业已经开始把它引入研发流程。AI4S在哪个行业跑得更快，大致取决于两类条件。

一类是技术条件，AI给出的结果，能不能被快速、清楚地验证。另一类是产业条件，行业愿不愿意引入外部技术，新成果进入生产的门槛有多高，核心数据和研发流程是否掌握在企业自己手里。两类条件同时具备的行业很少，目前跑在前面的，往往只占了其中一头。

医药是产业条件最成熟的领域。

新药研发投入高、周期长、失败率高，从药物分子筛选到临床试验，可能需要十余年。如果能缩短早期研发时间、减少无效实验，就有理由尝试。

医药行业成熟的研发分工，也为AI公司留出了位置。药企长期采购专业软件，也习惯把部分研发工作外包给第三方机构。AI公司可以沿着现有的产业链切入，不必从头培养客户的付费习惯。

但入场早也意味着竞争更加激烈。国内已有晶泰科技、英矽智能、剂泰科技等AI制药上市公司，AI制药也经历了多轮投资热潮。叶亦天告诉「定焦One」，如今AI制药领域已经聚集了不少公司，要找到具有差异化能力的新项目并不容易。

资本开始寻找下一个方向，材料成为最受关注的方向之一。

材料的优势在技术条件。新配方是否提高稳定性、新材料是否改善导电性能，都可以通过具体指标判断，验证周期比新药短得多。电池、芯片、化工等产业都有材料研发需求，AI可以帮助企业预测材料性能、缩小筛选范围，减少反复试错的成本。

一些AI材料公司也已经拿到大额融资。今年7月，AI材料公司深度原理完成A系列融资，累计融资金额近10亿元，业务覆盖营养日化、精细化工、新能源等领域。

光学是投资人眼中另一个值得关注的方向。叶亦天提到，半导体制造中的光刻和检测、医疗设备、光通信、新能源等领域，都需要复杂的光学设计和计算，其中有大量仿真和参数优化工作，为AI提供了应用空间。他认为，光学相关技术可以覆盖多个产业，具备较大的市场潜力。

还有一些行业，技术需求明确，却很难长出独立的AI4S公司。

半导体设计是一个例子，芯片企业长期使用EDA软件完成设计、仿真和验证，核心设计数据、研发流程和专业人才通常掌握在芯片公司及工业软件企业内部。核聚变则高度依赖大型科研装置、专业团队，创业公司很难直接参与核心研发。

叶亦天将AI4S的机会分成两类：材料、生物医药等领域，有机会诞生独立提供模型、研发服务或软硬件产品的公司；而半导体设计、核聚变等方向，AI可能更多成为既有产业的一项核心研发能力。

同样是AI4S，放在不同行业里，起跑线差别很大。

04 理想很大，生意还早

选对了行业，创业者们还要回答一个更现实的问题：这门生意能不能赚到钱？

目前，AI4S公司主要有两种收入来源：卖科研工具、帮客户完成研发任务。

科理新序选择了前者，希望将生命科学基座模型和科研智能体做成科研工具。Erik告诉「定焦One」，目前公司面向高校、科研院所的产品全部免费，降低科研人员接触先进AI技术的门槛；同时在推进企业付费合作，未来通过科学基座模型的API，科学评测标准、药物研发成果等产品获得收入。

智源深澜则已经通过承接研发项目获得收入。客户包括大型药企、中小型药企以及生物技术公司，它们提出研发需求，智源深澜利用AI模型和自动化实验平台完成分子设计、筛选、优化等工作，再按照项目收费。

但两家公司都不打算只卖工具和服务。王承志设想，智源深澜未来还可以利用AI自主研发药物，再把候选药物及相关知识产权授权给大型药企。在医药行业，有价值的候选药物可以通过技术授权获得首付款，并根据后续研发、临床和销售进展，获得里程碑付款及收益分成。成功的授权交易，潜在回报可能远高于单个研发服务项目。

Erik认为，如果未来AI能够独立发现新分子、新材料，甚至创造具有广泛应用价值的新技术，创业公司的收入便有机会从出售科研工具，延伸到出售科研成果。

但让AI从提高科研效率，到拿出能够被产业认可的成果，中间还有很长一段路。

资本对这段时间差的耐心并不一致。一位接触过多家AI4S项目的FA告诉「定焦One」，一些早期投资机构愿意给科研项目探索空间，即使公司尚未形成收入，也可以先投资技术和团队。另一些机构则希望企业在A轮前后，就拿出明确的商业化验证或阶段性成果。不同赛道的要求也有差异。材料领域的项目如果半年或一年内拿不出可验证的进展，投资人可能产生疑虑。而量子计算等研发周期更长的前沿领域，通常能获得更长的观察期。

在叶亦天看来，投资人最看重三件事。一是团队要有AI和科学的复合背景，只懂算法、不懂行业，很难做出有竞争力的产品。二是能否积累高质量的数据，无论通过专业算法、自动化实验还是产业合作，这决定了模型质量和技术壁垒。三是有没有真实客户持续买单。早期公司收入可以不大，但产品要已经卖给有长期研发需求的企业，且能形成复购。至于卖的是工具还是服务，并没有绝对的优劣，“有人买单就有价值”。

留给创业公司的时间也未必充裕。前述FA提到，有AI4S创业者判断，国内部分AI4S初创公司可能只有1至1.5年的窗口期。眼下，国内通用模型厂商仍把大量资源投入基础模型、编程和通用Agent，专业科研领域还留有创业空间。但如果大厂进一步加码AI4S，创业公司的先发优势可能受到挑战。

窗口期有限，长期投入又不可省。现阶段，AI4S公司赚的主要是科研提效的钱，科学发现这门更大的生意还在前方。在那之前，创业公司还要跑得再快一些。

05 结语

AI4S的“ChatGPT时刻”来了吗？

在Erik看来，它已经发生了。谷歌DeepMind的AlphaFold破解蛋白质结构预测难题，拿下诺贝尔奖，让整个科学界看到了AI改变科研的可能。如今这么多人才和资本涌入，正是因为大家相信了这一点。

王承志对AlphaFold的感受则更平静一些。他至今记得第一次用ChatGPT时的震撼，但在AI4S领域，他还没有体会过。AlphaFold的到来，是多年技术积累和持续迭代的结果，模型达到预期后，科研人员很快又将注意力转向它尚未解决的问题，难以感受到很大的变革。

这或许正是科学进步的常态。王承志说，人们往往很难准确感知自己正身处怎样的技术变化之中。就像几年前，人们难以想象AI能够完成复杂的编程、数学任务。如今，这些能力已经成为寻常，人们反而开始觉得AI还不够聪明。

AI4S的“ChatGPT时刻”，或许不会以一声巨响的方式到来。王承志曾给出一个大胆预测，未来七八年，AI可能接管大部分科学发现工作。

到那时回头看，人们或许才会意识到，那个时刻早已悄悄来过。

title: Advocating for your own health starts when nothing hurts
summary: “Nothing hurts. I feel fine. Why would I need to see a doctor?” Throughout my career, I have heard variations of these words many times. But I have also heard them outside of my profession...
full_content:
“Nothing hurts. I feel fine. Why would I need to see a doctor?”

Throughout my career, I have heard variations of these words many times. But I have also heard them outside of my professional life, in conversations with family and friends. And I understand the reasoning behind them. When we feel well, we assume that everything is fine. We do things, take care of our families, manage our responsibilities, and move through our daily routines. Making a doctor’s appointment when nothing seems wrong is often the last thing on our minds.

Yet I must admit, it is difficult to watch someone you love continually put their health aside. Not because you want to tell them what to do, but because you care about them and want them to be well.

After more than twenty years working in clinical research, particularly in oncology, I have learned something that has stayed with me. Feeling fine does not always mean that everything is fine.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

Working in oncology has given me the opportunity to see health care from a perspective that goes far beyond clinical trials, protocols, and treatments. Behind every diagnosis is a person, a family, and a life that can change in ways no one anticipated. It has also made me think differently about the importance of paying attention to our bodies and recognizing when something deserves medical attention.

Take melanoma, for example. A mole that begins to change in size, shape, or color may not hurt. A new or unusual spot on the skin may seem insignificant. It is easy to assume that if something is not causing discomfort, there is no reason to be concerned.

Yet melanoma can develop without pain, and identifying it early can make a significant difference in treatment options and outcomes. This is why something as simple as noticing a change and scheduling an appointment with a dermatologist can matter. The same principle applies to many other aspects of our health, and even when we have no symptoms at all, recommended screenings and preventive appointments remain important.

I sometimes think about how much time we dedicate to everything else in our lives. We make time for volunteering, family obligations, and countless other responsibilities. We rearrange our schedules when something important comes up. But how often do we give our own health that same priority? How often do we tell ourselves that we will schedule an appointment next month, or after a project is finished, or when life becomes a little less busy? And how often does that next month turn into another six months or even a year?

I believe that advocating for our health means being attentive, asking questions, and understanding that we have an important role in our own care. We do not need a medical background to ask a physician why something is happening, whether additional evaluation is necessary, or what changes we should watch for. We should feel comfortable having those conversations. And if we do not understand something, we should ask again.

In oncology clinical research, I have learned that some of the most important conversations about health begin long before someone ever considers participating in a clinical trial. Those conversations may begin during a routine examination, after noticing an unfamiliar change, or simply by asking a question that has been on someone’s mind. But advocating for health does not have to stop with ourselves.

Sometimes, it is worth having that conversation with someone you love. Ask when they last had a checkup. Encourage them to make an appointment they have been postponing. And don’t let the conversation end there. Follow up with them. Ask whether they were able to schedule the appointment. Perhaps offer to go with them if they would feel more comfortable having someone by their side.

Sometimes, a little encouragement, a reminder, or simply being there can make a meaningful difference. Of course, we cannot make decisions for other people. But we can remind them that their health matters, that they matter, and that they do not have to navigate every concern alone.

The purpose of advocating for our health is not to guarantee an outcome. It is to give ourselves the opportunity to recognize concerns, seek appropriate care, and make informed decisions.

Being more than two decades in clinical research, I have tremendous respect for the courage people demonstrate when facing uncertainty about their health. Their experiences have also reinforced something I carry with me outside of my professional life.

Our health deserves our attention before it demands it.

Perhaps there is a screening you have been meaning to schedule. Perhaps you have noticed something different but have not found the time to discuss it. Or perhaps it has simply been a while since your last routine appointment. And perhaps there is someone you love who needs a little encouragement to do the same.

Make the appointment. Have the conversation. Follow up with someone you care about. Not because something is necessarily wrong. But because our health, and the health of those we love, deserves attention even when nothing hurts.

Sometimes, advocating for health begins with making that appointment. And sometimes, it begins with helping someone you love make theirs.

Regina Portnoy is a clinical research professional.

title: Private equity in psychiatry puts continuity of care at risk
summary: I treat people whose illnesses don’t resolve in a few visits. Many of my patients have depression that hasn’t responded to several medications, or OCD that has shaped their lives for decad...
full_content:
I treat people whose illnesses don’t resolve in a few visits. Many of my patients have depression that hasn’t responded to several medications, or OCD that has shaped their lives for decades. Getting them better takes time, and it takes knowing them well. So I’ve watched with some unease as mental health care has become a favorite target for investors. I should say up front that I own a small independent psychiatry practice and now compete with several groups backed by private equity, so I have a stake in this. I’ve tried to let the evidence carry the argument.

By 2022, about 6.2 percent of U.S. mental health facilities were owned by private equity, and the buying has since spread to psychiatric hospitals. The playbook is no secret. A firm buys a practice, loads it with debt, cuts costs, pushes revenue, and plans to sell within a few years, usually fewer than seven. Capital can do real good. It can pay for better information systems, make recruiting easier, and keep a struggling practice from closing. My concern is timing. Someone with bipolar disorder, treatment-resistant depression, or early psychosis needs care measured in years, while a fund’s exit strategy is measured in quarters. Patients and families deserve to know which of those two clocks their care runs on.

The research we have so far should make all of us cautious. A systematic review of 55 studies in the BMJ found that private equity ownership was most consistently tied to higher costs for patients and payers, with mixed to harmful effects on quality and no consistent benefit. Hospitals acquired by private equity saw a 25 percent relative increase in preventable hospital-acquired conditions compared with matched hospitals.

We have much less data specific to psychiatry. Part of the reason is that many acquisitions don’t have to be disclosed, and nondisclosure agreements are common. To me, that gap is a reason to look harder. Psychiatric patients are vulnerable, and they are often cared for in settings where outsiders can see very little and patients have few choices. In a 2026 position paper, the American College of Physicians urged policymakers to protect clinical autonomy and to make sure physicians keep control over patient care.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

When doctors talk about autonomy, it can sound like we’re protecting our turf. I understand that reaction. But in my experience, autonomy is how a patient’s needs actually make it into the exam room. It means the psychiatrist who knows the patient decides whether a medication change calls for a full hour or a quick fifteen minutes, whether a stable patient can safely come in less often, and whether a crisis is worth clearing the afternoon for.

Productivity models built on billable units and session counts are easy to track. They also tend to miss the quality of care, and they have been linked to clinician burnout, turnover, and pressure toward ethically questionable practices. Physicians employed by organizations that private equity has acquired report lower satisfaction and less autonomy, and they are less likely to stay with their employer. In many fields, turnover is mostly a staffing problem. In psychiatry, when a doctor leaves, the patient loses the therapeutic relationship too.

That relationship is the treatment. Continuity of care has long been considered essential for people with serious mental illness. It has been associated with better social functioning, quality of life, and symptom control, although study methods vary. When you ask patients with long-term mental illness what they value most, they keep giving the same answer, and it’s continuity.

Care built to scale depends on protocolized visits, rotating clinicians, and handing work to whoever costs least. On a spreadsheet that can look efficient. In the room, it slowly wears away the knowledge that keeps patients safe: what this person’s last relapse looked like, which side effect nearly made them stop treatment, and what “I’m fine” really means when they say it. Data from the Veterans Health Administration point the same way. Adequate staffing predicted better mental health treatment quality, access, continuity, and satisfaction more strongly than productivity metrics did.

I’m not claiming that every practice backed by investors does harm, or that every independent practice is excellent. Ownership doesn’t decide outcomes by itself. Incentives do shape them, and patients have every right to ask about those incentives.

I don’t support psychiatry led by physicians out of nostalgia. I support it because it leaves decisions with the person who is accountable for how the patient does. In a field where the relationship does so much of the healing, that arrangement is worth defending.

Ravi Singareddy is the founder and medical director of Empower Psychiatry & Sleep in north metro Atlanta, where he leads an interventional psychiatry practice offering transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) and Spravato (esketamine) for treatment-resistant depression. Double board-certified in psychiatry and sleep medicine, he brings more than two decades of clinical and academic experience to patients who haven’t found relief with medications alone. He is affiliated with Emory Healthcare.

His interest in neuromodulation dates back to his years as associate professor of psychiatry at Penn State College of Medicine. There, he taught annually on vagus nerve stimulation and novel depression therapies, and he published on long-term combined electroconvulsive therapy and vagus nerve stimulation in the American Journal of Psychiatry. He has authored numerous peer-reviewed papers on sleep disorders, insomnia, anxiety, and depression, with work appearing in Sleep, the Journal of Clinical Sleep Medicine, and Psychiatry Research.

Singareddy is a Fellow of the American Psychiatric Association and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and practices measurement-based care, tracking outcomes to guide every treatment decision. He shares updates on Instagram.

title: 独家专访浩博医药CEO程国锋：从吉利德到浩博，攻坚乙肝功能性治愈
summary: 浩博医药CEO程国锋专访揭示其乙肝功能性治愈研发进展。针对现有疗法需终身服药的痛点，公司自主研发的反义寡核苷酸药物AHB-137在2026年AASLD年会上公布重磅数据：NA经治及初治患者停药15个月后，功能性治愈维持率极高，部分患者应答进一步改善，持久应答率超90%，获专家高度认可。目前该药已进入III期临床，标志着从早期探索迈向关键后期阶段。程国锋凭借在吉利德参与丙肝治愈药物研发的深厚经验，联...
full_content:
撰稿 | 朱萍、武瑛港


慢性乙型肝炎治疗长期面临一个难题：现有核苷（酸）类似物能够有效抑制病毒复制，却很难帮助患者摆脱长期甚至终身服药。对于患者而言，治疗期间控制住病毒只是第一步，停药之后能否继续维持应答，才是衡量功能性治愈价值的重要标准。

 

2026年美国肝病研究学会（AASLD）年会上，浩博医药自主研发的反义寡核苷酸（ASO）乙肝治疗药物AHB-137公布了两项长期随访研究结果，分别覆盖NA经治和初治患者，并同时入选最新突破口头报告（Late-breaking Oral）。结果显示AHB-137治疗后实现的功能性治愈可持久维持：在完成相应访视评估的核苷（酸）类似物（NA）经治和初治参与者中，分别有9/9例和6/6例在停用全部抗乙肝病毒治疗后15个月仍维持功能性治愈；部分原为部分应答（PR）的参与者在停药后应答进一步改善，转化为完全应答（CR）。

 

对于有限疗程治疗而言，停药后的持久性恰恰是衡量临床价值的重要维度。南方医科大学南方医院侯金林教授在接受《感染在线》采访时表示，AHB-137长期随访中达到完全应答并停用全部治疗的患者，持久应答率超过90%，这一结果为功能性治愈的长期维持提供了新的证据。

 

目前AHB-137已进入III期临床。从2023年首次进入临床I期到关键数据即将揭晓，浩博正将一条早期探索的技术路线推向临床后期。这一进程背后，既有创始团队此前在丙肝治愈药物研发中积累的经验，也有围绕患者需求对临床开发、研究设计和药物质量所做的持续投入。近日，我们独家专访浩博医药联合创始人、CEO程国锋，了解一款乙肝创新药的研发进展，以及中国小核酸团队如何在实践中推动产业能力建设。

 


程国锋对乙肝功能性治愈的探索，始于此前在吉利德的研发经历。他拥有美国伊利诺伊大学芝加哥分校微生物学及免疫学博士学位，博士后师从Scripps研究所Frank Chisari，曾担任吉利德科学公司抗病毒新药研发高级总监，参与Harvoni、Epclusa和Vosevi等丙肝治愈药物的发现与早期开发，也主导过多项乙肝创新药物研发。

 

这段经历让程国锋和后来共同创业的杨成勇，对创新药研发有了更完整的认识。他们不仅参与药物发现，也接触临床开发、CMC及后续研究，理解一款药物从实验室走向患者，需要科学、临床、生产和监管等多个环节协同推进。丙肝治愈药物的成功，也让他们看到，重大传染性疾病的治疗格局有可能被创新药改变。

 

2019年，两人决定回国创业，将新的研发目标指向乙肝。与丙肝不同，乙肝病毒感染涉及复杂的病毒学和免疫学机制。现有NA药物能够抑制病毒复制，却难以清除病毒抗原，也很难帮助患者摆脱长期治疗。如何在降低病毒抗原的同时，推动患者自身免疫系统重新建立对病毒的控制，是实现功能性治愈需要回答的关键问题。

 

当时，行业对小核酸技术的关注更多集中在siRNA等方向，ASO并不是最受追捧的路线。真正让程国锋和杨成勇看到探索价值的，是ASO早期的临床研究数据提示的早期研究信号。虽然这些研究尚不足以证明一条成熟的治疗路径，部分机制和临床前结果也存在需要进一步验证的问题，但它们提示了一个可能性：ASO除了降低病毒抗原，是否还能够在特定条件下产生免疫相关作用？

 

“我们看到的这两组数据，都给了我们灵感。”程国锋回忆。团队没有把早期信号直接当作结论，而是将其转化为科学假设，通过机制研究、实验验证和临床研究逐步寻找答案。浩博选择从乙肝切入，核心并不是追逐技术热点，而是希望围绕一个长期未得到充分满足的临床需求，找到新的治疗路径。

 

此后，AHB-137逐步从早期研发走向临床。浩博在推进候选药物的同时，也持续完善临床开发、药学研究和质量控制体系。随着临床数据不断积累，项目从早期探索进入更大规模的临床验证阶段。2025年，AHB-137获准在中国开展III期临床研究，标志着这款药物进入新的开发阶段。

 

对一家成立仅七年的创新药公司而言，这一进展体现了研发团队的执行效率，也离不开持续的资源投入。浩博从早期个人投资支持起步，随后随着临床数据逐渐积累，获得专业机构认可；截至2026年8月，公司已完成C轮融资，累计融资3.6亿美元。资金持续投入到临床研究、工艺开发和研发能力建设中，为AHB-137进入临床后期提供了支撑。

 

七年时间，浩博完成了从科学假设到临床后期开发的重要跨越。对于程国锋而言，这一进展既是对最初研发判断的阶段性验证，也意味着团队需要继续以临床证据回答更重要的问题：AHB-137能否让患者获得持久的功能性治愈？有限疗程治疗的价值，最终又该如何通过严谨的临床研究来证明？

 


对于乙肝功能性治愈药物而言，治疗结束后的应答维持情况，是判断临床价值的重要维度。患者真正期待的并不只是治疗期间病毒指标下降，而是在完成有限疗程后，能够在停止所有乙肝治疗的情况下，继续维持对病毒的控制。

 

这也是浩博此次在AASLD公布长期随访数据的意义所在。两项报告均基于AB-10-8004长期随访研究，纳入此前AHB-137 II期研究中达到完全应答或部分应答的患者，分别观察NA经治人群和初治人群停用所有乙肝治疗后的应答持久性及长期安全性。

 

研究对完全应答有明确界定：乙肝表面抗原（HBsAg）低于0.05 IU/mL，且HBV DNA低于定量下限。停用所有乙肝治疗后持续维持完全应答至少24周，才符合功能性治愈的标准。对于进入长期随访时仍在接受NA治疗的患者，研究还会评估其是否符合停药标准，并在安全性监测下实施停药。

 

在NA经治人群中，既往II期研究达到完全应答的21名患者中，有18人在原研究阶段已经停止NA治疗。进入长期随访后，在有可用数据的患者中，16/17例在停用所有乙肝治疗12个月后仍维持功能性治愈；完成15个月评估的9例患者，全部维持这一状态。另有3名在原研究阶段尚未停用NA的完全应答患者，也在长期随访期间停止了NA治疗，其中1人已完成停药后9个月随访并维持功能性治愈。

 

初治人群的数据同样值得关注。既往研究中达到完全应答的7名患者，在停用AHB-137后9个月时有6人维持功能性治愈；继续随访的6名患者，在停药后15个月时仍全部维持这一状态。

 

需要强调的是，这些数据来自既往II期研究中达到完全应答或部分应答的特定患者群体，并不代表所有接受AHB-137治疗患者的总体治愈率。不同队列的样本量和随访时间也有所差异。但从研究问题来看，这些结果提供了一个重要观察：对于治疗阶段已经达到完全应答的患者，停止所有乙肝治疗后，部分患者能够在较长时间内维持功能性治愈。

 

南方医科大学南方医院侯金林教授认为，对于长期接受NA治疗的患者，停药后应答能否持久维持，是衡量治疗价值的关键因素。吉林大学第一医院牛俊奇教授则指出，初治患者仍有大量未被满足的临床需求，有限疗程治疗如果能够实现功能性治愈，有望为这一人群提供新的治疗选择。

 

浩博医药联合创始人、首席科学官杨成勇从机制角度给出了进一步解释：当HBsAg被深度抑制后，患者能否依靠自身免疫系统在停药后持续控制病毒，是研究试图回答的关键科学问题。部分应答者在停药后进一步转为完全应答，也提示治疗结束后，宿主免疫可能仍在持续发挥作用。这与AHB-137通过降低HBsAg、促进抗病毒免疫恢复的设计理念相呼应。

 

对程国锋而言，临床研究的意义不仅在于取得积极数据，更在于让研究设计始终围绕患者真正关心的问题展开。对于一款瞄准功能性治愈的药物，治疗期间的应答、停药后的持久性以及长期安全性，需要放在同一条证据链中考察。只有回答了这些问题，才能判断有限疗程治疗是否有可能成为患者新的选择。

 

当然，长期随访数据仍需要在更大规模的临床研究中进一步验证。此次研究总体安全性良好，未观察到严重ALT升高、肝功能失代偿或新的迟发性安全信号，但这并不意味着患者停药后无需监测。功能性治愈并不等于病毒彻底清除，停药后的随访和长期肝脏健康管理仍然重要。

 

目前，AHB-137正在中国开展III期临床研究。对浩博来说，下一阶段需要在更大规模患者中继续验证疗效和安全性，并进一步明确获益人群、治疗方案及停药后的管理路径。程国锋将2027年提交NDA作为公司的开发目标，但最终进度仍取决于临床研究结果和监管审评。相比单纯追求开发速度，他更强调在推进效率与数据质量之间取得平衡，让每一步临床进展都能够为药物的最终价值提供可靠依据。

 


AHB-137能够从早期研发走向III期，除了分子本身的研发进展，也离不开药物生产、分析方法、质量控制和监管沟通等环节的持续完善。对浩博而言，这些工作既是推进产品开发的必要条件，也是在国内小核酸产业尚处于发展阶段时，通过真实项目积累研发经验的过程。

 

2019年前后，国内小核酸药物研发的产业配套还不成熟，尤其在CMC、分析方法和质量控制方面，许多环节缺乏成熟经验。浩博在推进AHB-137的过程中，与合作方共同摸索生产工艺。程国锋也亲自参与合作沟通和工艺问题讨论，遇到生产环节的技术问题，双方会反复研究、调整，有时讨论持续到深夜。

 

小核酸药物的CMC开发涉及合成工艺、纯化、杂质控制、分析方法和质量标准等多个环节。随着临床研究推进，药物生产不仅要满足早期临床试验需求，还要具备支持更大规模研究的稳定性和可控性。浩博与合作方在项目中共同解决这些问题，逐步积累工艺开发和质量控制经验。

 

GLP毒理和生物分析同样如此。面对当时国内相关研究经验不足的情况，浩博与合作方共同摸索小核酸药物的毒理评价方法，并投入资金购置仪器，在公司内部建立小核酸生物分析方法。这项工作由杨成勇带领团队完成，建立的方法后来也用于支持合作方的相关研究。

 

这些实践的价值并不局限于AHB-137。对小核酸药物而言，临床开发需要药学、非临床和临床证据相互支撑，生产工艺、分析方法和质量控制能力也需要随着项目进展同步完善。浩博在一个具体产品上积累的经验，为后续小核酸项目开发提供了可借鉴的基础，也让合作伙伴在共同解决问题的过程中积累了新的技术经验。

 

产业能力建设之外，监管沟通也是浩博持续投入的工作。程国锋和杨成勇在吉利德参与丙肝药物研发时，曾与FDA进行多轮沟通。这段经历让他们认识到，监管沟通不应只是产品申报前的程序性工作，而应该贯穿药物研发全过程。企业需要理解监管机构关注的问题，也要尽早把自己的科学判断、临床设计和数据证据摆出来，通过持续交流减少信息差。

 

“我们企业需要理解监管机构关注什么，也要尽早把自己的科学判断、临床设计和数据证据摆出来。”程国锋表示。

 

在AHB-137的开发过程中，浩博持续与监管机构沟通，并在获得关键临床数据后，通过国际学术会议向行业公开。对创新药研发而言，公开数据意味着接受学术界的检验，也有助于让监管机构和临床研究者更早了解项目进展。尤其对于小核酸这样的新兴技术领域，企业需要通过扎实的药学、非临床和临床证据，逐步建立对新技术的理解与信任。

 

从工艺开发、分析方法到监管沟通，浩博围绕AHB-137所做的工作，实际上是在补齐一款小核酸药物从研发走向临床所需的关键环节。它们并不一定都能在短期内体现为产品进度上的直接突破，却构成了创新药高质量开发的基础。随着更多小核酸药物进入临床，这些经验也有机会转化为行业可以借鉴的能力。

 

浩博目前仍将乙肝功能性治愈作为核心方向，在推进AHB-137的同时，探索后续管线和联合治疗方案，并持续建设小核酸技术平台。对于未来，程国锋希望浩博成为全球乙肝功能性治愈领域的重要参与者，而不只是被看作一家小核酸技术公司。患者能否真正从创新中获益，是他反复强调的判断标准。药物不仅要研发出来，还要考虑未来如何通过临床证据、生产供应和市场准入，让更多患者获益。

 

从吉利德到浩博，程国锋希望带回中国的，不只是参与丙肝治愈药物研发的经验，更是一套围绕临床需求推进创新药开发的方法。七年时间，AHB-137从早期研发走到III期，浩博也在临床研究、监管沟通和产业协作中逐步形成自己的研发能力。接下来，III期研究还将继续检验药物的疗效与安全性，但这七年的进展已经显示出一条清晰的路径：以未满足的临床需求为起点，以严谨的临床证据为依据，在推进速度的同时守住研发质量，并在解决患者问题的过程中推动产业能力向前发展。

title: 【首发】无界进化完成超亿元Pre-A轮融资，刷新中国AI虚拟细胞企业单笔融资金额纪录

full_content:
动脉网第一时间获悉，11月16日，以虚拟细胞与递归科学发现为核心的AI for Science（科学智能，AI4S）企业无界进化（INFevo）宣布完成超亿元Pre-A轮融资，刷新中国虚拟细胞企业单笔融资金额纪录。


本轮由星连资本、Prosperity7、华盖资本、华控基金及德同资本等机构联合投资，老股东顺为资本、红杉中国和松禾资本继续追加投资。这是公司继2026年6月完成数千万元天使轮融资后，五个月内完成的第二轮融资。


资金将加快公司AI4S基础设施建设，推动细胞响应预测、科学假说检验与高通量自动化实验反馈的深度协同，打造覆盖“靶点发现—虚拟筛选—临床方案优化”的全链路AI生物学平台，加速前沿计算向疾病精准干预与创新临床疗法的转化。


1以“递归科学发现”打通“大模型＋自动化实验”双驱闭环


AI在生物医药领域的应用正从分子设计拓展至细胞及系统生物学层面的动态研究，以更高效地探索药物、基因等干预如何改变复杂的生命系统。然而，随着探索空间的指数级扩大，计算端生成假说的能力与传统湿实验验证能力之间出现严重的效率与通量错配。


面对湿实验验证瓶颈，AI驱动的虚拟细胞模型及高通量自动化实验室有望成为破局的关键技术之一。模型可以在实验前预测药物或基因干预引起的细胞变化，并以此推测药物在更复杂生物系统，包括动物及人体内的效果，帮助研究者筛选候选分子、比较潜在靶点，并确定实验优先级，让有限的实验资源用于检验更有价值的方向，从而大幅提升早期发现的转化效率，加速靶点发现与生物学机制解析的进程。


 

随着 AI 与自动化技术推动研发效率升级，科研体系的深层瓶颈也愈发凸显：科学发现过程中形成的知识、分析方法和负结果经验往往散落、流失在孤立的项目中，难以沉淀为可复用的组织资产，导致科研探索长期陷于低效的重复试错。如何让这些中间研究成果突破孤岛，实现规模化积累，并持续用于模型迭代、假说生成和实验设计及验证，成为AI4S从单点效率提升走向系统性发现能力跃迁的关键。


对此，无界进化提出递归科学发现（Recursive scientific discovery, RSD）理念。递归自我提升（Recursive self-improvement, RSI）聚焦AI系统自身的能力改进，RSD 则将持续提升延伸至科学发现的全过程。该体系通过对科学问题、假说推演、分析方法与实验结果进行结构化留存、关联和复用，使记录的证据与经验持续驱动后续的假说生成、实验设计和候选筛选。


 

基于 RSD 框架，无界进化构建了“AI基础大模型＋高通量自动化实验”的双驱闭环体系。这一体系的一端是覆盖细胞多组学的无界进化自研基础大模型OCOO，用于预测药物、基因等干预引起的细胞响应；另一端是涵盖细胞培养、扰动和多组学检测的自动化湿实验体系，用于检验关键预测并产生新数据。模型辅助确定更具潜力的实验方向，实验结果则用于检验预测、改进模型，并指导后续研究。二者通过统一的数据与研究产物管理机制衔接，让每次探索积累的证据与经验持续用于改进系统的预测与实验设计能力。



依托上述底层架构，无界进化在成立数月内围绕靶点发现、虚拟筛选与临床前评估等核心场景取得领先成果，推动相关能力从模型研发走向真实的研究场景。


在模型研发方面，公司已发布OCOO系列中基于转录组数据的虚拟细胞基础模型OCOO-T，直接对细胞在各类扰动下的基因表达变化进行建模，以简洁、可扩展的模型架构，实现跨扰动类型的统一建模与领先的预测表现。


在三大单细胞扰动权威基准——Tahoe100M、Replogle和PBMC的同条件评测中，OCOO-T均取得行业领先表现，为其用于模拟真实扰动生物学、支撑靶点发现与早期药效评价奠定了坚实的基础。


在科研产品方面，无界进化以提出科学“证伪主义”的哲学家卡尔·波普尔（Karl Popper）命名，推出可自主迭代的科学假说挖掘引擎The Popper Project（TPP）。TPP接入专业科研智能体与多源专业数据库，生成、质疑和完善可检验的假说，并以可追溯的推理链呈现证据、标明缺口、提出实验建议。平台支持科学家共同评议、补充证据，推动假说随研究反馈持续演进；未来还将接入虚拟细胞模型，进一步衔接假说生成、计算推演、独立复核与湿实验验证。


TPP平台搭载的Karl Workbench 科研工作台已开启内测，首次将RSD理念落实为面向科学家的日常研究工具。工作台围绕记录、积累、产物、监督、进化五项系统能力，将科学问题与假说进一步连接到数据、分析、实验与可复现执行的完整工作流。研究者可以复核证据、审查关键判断并接续已有任务，任务轨迹、研究产物和历史经验得以跨越单次课题任务持续发挥作用，使整个科研团队的研究体系具备从自身历史中持续学习与自我演进的能力。


在10月份基于耶鲁大学、Broad研究所、哈佛大学、斯坦福大学等机构联合发布的科研Agent基准SciAgentArena开展的复测中，Karl Workbench在搭载DeepSeek基础模型的条件下，在单细胞组学与空间组学两大场景均获得综合得分第一，在本次评测范围内达到SOTA（行业最优）水平，表现优于包括Claude Code、Codex在内、搭载Opus 5、GPT-5.6 等当时前沿大模型的同类系统，展现出该系统在接近实际研究流程的科研任务中行业领先的系统级表现。

图：Karl Workbench在SciAgentArena单细胞组学与空间组学评测中得分位列第一


3连接前沿计算与真实应用场景：打造工业级AI生物学底座


在打通“计算—工具—实验”链条的同时，无界进化持续聚焦于真实疾病问题与药物研发场景，深度参与由北京大学第一医院牵头的“肝胆胰肿瘤类器官培养与智慧诊疗北京市重点实验室”共建。该合作以临床重大需求为牵引，旨在构建“临床问题—类器官模型—药物筛选—AI分析—临床验证”的研究体系。


作为实验室人工智能与虚拟细胞模型方向的核心支撑，无界进化将虚拟细胞模型能力系统性地接入患者来源的真实临床样本，推动AI预测与类器官实验验证的双向迭代，探索细胞响应预测在临床决策与新药筛选一线场景中的应用。


无界进化能够快速跨越初创企业的平台建设期，得益于孵化方晶泰科技（2228.HK）深厚的产业积累。晶泰科技十余年沉淀的底层研发经验、上下游生态与全球产业网络，为无界进化提供了兼具高起点与强产业落地基因的成长土壤。


在技术层面，无界进化的虚拟细胞与晶泰科技横跨多种药物模态的分子设计及自动化合成能力高度协同互补，有望形成“分子生成—细胞响应预测—湿实验验证”的跨尺度闭环。晶泰科技的孵化与生态赋能不仅加速了无界进化技术体系的建设，也使预测模型从研发之初就面向真实的药物管线研发需求与严格的工业级标准。


本轮所募资金将重点用于无界进化的基础大模型研发、高通量自动化干湿闭环体系扩容，以及产业生态的深化建设。


未来，公司将携手全球药企、医院与科研机构，推动其技术与产品进入日常科研与产业研发的一线场景，解析复杂疾病干预机制，提升新药研发效率基线，共同拓展生命科学领域的认知与干预边界。


晶泰科技联合创始人、首席创新官，无界进化联合创始人赖力鹏表示：“药物研发的尺度，既在于分子工程的精度，更在于人类对复杂生命与疾病机制理解的深度。当高维生物学数据与前沿AI技术交汇，我们正迎来系统性破译生命语言、拓宽人类自我认知边界的关键拐点。


无界进化（INFevo）致力于将海量生物学数据、大模型与自进化方法深度耦合，打造原生AI生物学底座，向内打通虚拟细胞、自动化实验与AI递归科学发现能力，向外全面赋能药企、医院与科研院所，并与晶泰科技及众多生态伙伴深度协同，以此提升全球创新药研发的确定性，让更高效的疗法加速抵达患者身边。”


无界进化联合创始人赵亚龙表示：“感谢新老股东的信任与支持。依托本轮融资，无界进化（INFevo）将继续夯实‘基础大模型＋自动化实验’的干湿闭环基础设施，加速建设递归科学发现（RSD）系统，让实验数据持续推动模型与系统进化。我们期待携手科研与产业伙伴，将对生命的更深理解转化为药物创新的实际突破，加快从靶点发现到临床转化的进程，为尚未被攻克的疾病开辟新的治疗路径。”


星连资本表示：“AI与生命科学的深度融合，将成为下一轮科技创新的重要浪潮。生物系统具有极高的复杂性，也蕴藏着巨大的科学发现与产业创新空间。无界进化团队致力于将人工智能的建模与推理能力引入生命科学，通过将多模态数据、基础模型与实验体系的结合，探索 AI 理解生命、预测生命并推动生命科学研究的新路径。这是一条充满挑战但长期价值巨大的赛道，我们很高兴能够支持无界进化持续探索，也期待团队以扎实的技术积累和持续的工程创新，推动 AI for Biology从科研突破走向更广泛的产业应用。”


Prosperity7 Ventures表示：“细胞级模拟为以分子为核心的 AI 药物设计提供了进一步方案，有望解决从基础研究向临床成果转化过程中的各类难题。无界进化基于人工智能的虚拟细胞系统，正是为推动这一路径的发展而打造。我们很高兴能够支持公司开展技术研发并最终实现虚拟细胞的愿景。”


华盖资本表示：“无界进化真正的价值在于借助虚拟细胞体系与波普尔计划（TPP）打开全新的生物探索边界，突破传统研发难以触达的未知靶点发现瓶颈，这也是当下 AI 制药乃至整个制药行业最富挑战、最值得期待的方向。我们很高兴能够参与其中，见证‘无界进化’。”


松禾资本表示：“随着‘低垂果实’类的新靶点日益稀缺，行业迫切需要从经验驱动向数据与模型驱动转型。虚拟细胞模型模拟这种‘扰动—响应’的系统级结果，价值不仅在于大幅缩短研发周期、提升转化效率，更在于其有望打破传统认知边界，从海量数据中挖掘出更深层次的生物学机制与潜在关联。这将为发现全新靶点提供革命性工具，从根本上提高新药开发的成功率。我们非常期待并支持无界在这一前沿赛道上持续深耕。”



北京无界进化科技有限公司（INFevo）致力于构建行业领先的 AI 虚拟细胞模型，为全球药物创新提供变革性的生物学研究工具。公司整合生物领域最先进（SOTA）的自研基础大模型 OCOO 与自动化、智能化的细胞实验平台，打造全球领先的 AI 时代生物医药创新研究平台，从而有力支撑基础生物学的科研突破。


同时，公司还通过有效衔接临床研究，加速创新成果的落地转化。围绕抗衰老、神经退行性疾病、自身免疫疾病、代谢疾病、肿瘤等具有挑战性的研究方向，无界进化正加速建立起一套覆盖新机制与新靶点发现、虚拟药物筛选与评价，以及临床方案优化的全功能 AI 生物学平台。

title: Alert fatigue: Why doctors ignore up to 96 percent of EHR alerts [PODCAST]
summary: Listen and followApple PodcastsSpotifyYouTubeMore apps · Browse all episodes Doctors click past most of the alerts their electronic health record throws at them, and the industry has long blamed the d...
full_content:
Listen and followApple PodcastsSpotifyYouTubeMore apps · Browse all episodes

Doctors click past most of the alerts their electronic health record throws at them, and the industry has long blamed the doctors for it. Thomas Powell is a physician executive and a chief medical information officer. This episode is based on his article “Alert fatigue is a design problem, not a vigilance problem,” published on KevinMD. You will hear why a medical alert is blown right through 49 to 96 percent of the time, why he says that number says more about the system than about physicians, and how the alerts that matter get buried among the ones that do not. You will hear how he uses alert data to separate important from unimportant alerts, why every alert should come with an action item, and why most organizations never retire the alerts that came out of the box. You will also learn why turning off an alert is literally the flip of a switch yet rarely happens, why every alert needs a clinical owner, and why physicians who skip governance meetings end up living with decisions made for them. Press play for how to make the alerts that matter stand out again.

If this episode helped, follow The Podcast by KevinMD on Apple Podcasts or Spotify, and leave a rating.

Partner with me on the KevinMD platform. With more than 100 million impressions a year and nearly 750,000 followers, subscribers and email recipients across my channels, I give you direct access to the doctors and patients who matter most. Whether you need a sponsored article, email campaign, video interview, or a spot right here on the podcast, I offer the trusted space your brand deserves to be heard. Let’s work together to tell your story.

PARTNER WITH KEVINMD → https://kevinmd.com/influencer

SUBSCRIBE TO THE PODCAST → https://www.kevinmd.com/podcast

Transcript

Kevin Pho: Hi, and welcome to the show. Subscribe at KevinMD.com/podcast. Today, we welcome Thomas Powell. He is a physician executive and a career chief medical information officer. Today’s KevinMD article is “Alert fatigue is a design problem, not a vigilance problem.” Thomas, welcome to the show.

Thomas Powell: Well, thank you, Kevin. I look forward to this. I look forward to the discussion.

Kevin Pho: All right, let’s start by briefly sharing your story, then we’ll jump into why you decided to write this article on KevinMD.

Thomas Powell: OK. So as a physician, I went to medical school at University of Texas in San Antonio and did my residency at Duke in anesthesia. And while I was there was the NIH, National Library of Medicine fellowship, really sort of the beginning base of it for clinical informatics, and immediately I knew I had found what I wanted. So when I graduated there, my first role was at University of Miami, in the anesthesia department. I did both clinical and a lot of informatics work. And then really following that, I’ve been a chief medical information officer. I’ve been in academic centers; I’ve been at pediatrics, adult hospitals. I’ve put in Cerner; I’ve put in Epic. So that’s really where a lot of my energy has been, and actually trying to do the job well because informatics sort of got away from us when the HITECH Act was enacted as it was. Now I own my own LLC called CMIO LLC, where I’m consulting. I do interim executive work. I try to help people fix problems that they bring to me, and I do some industry consultation too. And then that brings me, and I just wrote a book that’s coming out on November 3, really putting it all together because really, as I was starting to put down thoughts of my life, I am concerned, and I think the concern is warranted. And I shared it a little bit, and other people that are reading it shared those concerns. So I thought it was very, very good. I’m happy to have done it.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

Kevin Pho: All right. So before we talk about alert fatigue in particular, one of the things that you mentioned earlier was that it’s important that CMIOs like yourself do their job well. Just in your terms, what does it mean for a CMIO to do their job well? There are so many aspects to that, so many intersections between health care and informatics. What does it mean to do their job well?

Thomas Powell: Well, and thank you for asking because that’s literally what the book is about. Clinical informatics is the name, and the role, chief medical information officer or chief health information officer, it’s been misunderstood. And a lot of people think of it as a technologic role. And what it is, is it’s a combination of four pretty significant skill sets that unfortunately are fairly rare to find, and people get installed without that ability to execute. So it’s really, you have to understand the technology, obviously. You have to understand the clinical aim. What are you trying to do with this clinical encounter? What are you trying to do with the thing that you’re executing? You have to understand workflow engineering because a lot of this is sort of manipulating both the clinician’s workflow, the way the clinic or inpatient unit flows, with what’s going on inside the EHR so that you can optimize the data. And really one of the big things, Kevin, that’s been a hard part of this is the executive empowerment. It’s very inconsistent how much energy a chief medical information officer has to actually protect the interests of the informatics, of the tool, of the clinical encounter. So I consider myself a physician to the system. That was how I always sort of explained it, is while the physicians are taking care of the patient, I’m trying to take care of the system that helps them take care of that patient. And that is really how I’ve always seen my role.

Kevin Pho: All right. Today we’re going to talk specifically about alert fatigue as a design problem, not a vigilance problem. Tell us why you decided to write this article, and for those that didn’t get a chance to read it, tell us about the article itself.

Thomas Powell: OK. So when you try to write down what was my focus, a big part of it is the physician experience. And there are a lot of things that your medical officer should be doing, and it’s going to be clinical in all different ways. But really, it’s about the physician experience, and alert fatigue is one of the big ones that just hasn’t been cracked yet. It’s basically the usability, and I’m sure you’ve heard the term now, which is physician wellness, where almost every organization is really putting a lot of energy into clinician wellness, but physician wellness specifically. And when you look at the data around physician wellness, physicians tend to report that it’s based upon two things. It’s their EHR causing them trouble, and it’s their HR causing them trouble. So it’s that combination of the work environment that you’re in and the EHR scores, and they’ve been terrible for a while. By the way, one of the most recent assessments was that the average physician rates their EHR experience at a 45.9 on a 100 scale, so an F. And it’s not that far different from where nurses are, which is even lower for nurses. So that’s not good. And really what the book tried to take on also was we’re aiming at our. So we have problems. Health care has had issues for a long time, and in ’99 when the Institute of Medicine came out and said about 98,000 people a year are actually killed in adverse events and things like that, everybody started saying, “OK, well, that’s what HITECH was about. We need an electronic health record.” But for why? Because I would not disagree with them, but they never aimed our technology at anything. It’s just put it in. And so what happens is you have a lot of hospital administrations and people thinking of the electronic health record as like a treatment. Like, it’s the thing that’s going to fix. It’s the solution. And actually, it’s more like an imaging modality. As a physician, I read it, and it tells me the image of what’s going on. I can actually, from the data, if I do this well, can reconstruct the workflows that are broken. I can reconstruct the workflows that are working. I can look at why things are the way they are. And so a big part of my heart was that a lot of people have for years blamed alert fatigue or blowing through alerts on the physicians. And so just to give you how bad it is, because this says more about the system. I think first off, I do want to back up and just say that whenever there’s been a study looking at what is going on from a clinical health, safety, and quality standpoint, the clinicians certainly have a part in it, but it’s a substantially smaller part than you believe. It always comes down to system. Almost every time, the system is the most heavily regarded contributor to adverse events, to all these things. And so when it comes down to alerts, the physician numbers are horrible. When you give a medical alert in an electronic health record system, 49 to 96 percent of the time it’s just blown right through. And that was interpreted by the industry, by the electronic health record industry, by IT, by administration as, “Well, look at those technophobes, the physicians that are not so happy with this, and they’re going to blow through all this.” And what I said, actually an alert, when I start distracting my physician from a clinical encounter, there’s actually an art to it. And so there’s a lot about the alerts themselves that are broken. There’s a lot about the volume of alerts that are broken. So that is the main thing. So I manage alerts. Wherever I go, I go in and I take both the pulse of the clinicians, but you can actually look at every alert. You can tell how many times it fired. You can tell which is being followed. And what you find out is many of these alerts are based on old advice. They’re sometimes now even conflicting. And now in the world of AI, you have these separate tools that are feeding in a whole nother world of alerts, advice, whatever. And what I believe is a central part of the quality safety issue is we have just confounded the clinical encounter. We’ve got a physician now doing data entry. We pay them; they spend 50 percent or more of their time doing data entry in today’s world. And they’re not doing a great job, which is because it was not their job. So they have a record that no one can use, even themselves. I hear that all the time because the notes are getting longer and longer and saying less and less. And the data that’s used, the whole idea was to get data that we could run the system and get better, be a learning health care organization and make our quality better, make our safety better, run our hospitals more efficiently, all those kinds of things. So the data is horrible. The physicians are burned out. Forty percent of physicians say that they are burned out, and it is related to their electronic health record experience.

Kevin Pho: And I agree with you. I have that firsthand knowledge. In my primary care clinic, in our electronic medical records, I would say almost always there’s some type of interaction, alert, boxes that obstruct me from executing my order. And if everything is alert, nothing is alert, right? So I think that that is definitely something that I face every day. Now, in your studies you said up to 96 percent of alerts are ignored, and among those 96 are some legitimate alerts, right? So from the patient’s standpoint, how does that harm patients, the fact that almost all of these alerts are blown through by clinicians?

Thomas Powell: Yeah. That’s actually a really important part of this, and the way that I frame it is it’s a problem that you’re making something and adding such inefficiency to the system, right? So we can talk about if you are just wasting my time, right, which is, that’s what that number’s saying. If I’m showing you a number of alerts that 96 percent of the time you ignore, something’s wrong. Right? But I say the real, the most important issue with it is that there’s no distinguishing feature to the important one, to the one that you’re going to miss. So buried inside of those, it’s not like everything that’s being told to you is unimportant. So that’s the thing, is the hope would be that you get to a world where I only let come through our system the alerts that help, right? I don’t need to teach you how to be a physician. You already know that part. And that’s unfortunately one of the things people did. They’re trying to remind you of how to, don’t forget this and don’t forget that, and administration would want you to do this. And so that’s where a lot of those, they’re overwhelmingly insignificant, even in the libraries of medication alerts. There’s a lot of drug interactions that, yes, theoretically or in some way it’s known that it does, but it’s an insignificant interaction. But if I get to you the right information that helps you make a good clinical decision, that is the goal, and you do that by aimed and targeted. And in a world of somebody blowing through 96 percent of the alerts, those just get blown through, and you find out about it when a clinical event happens. That’s sort of the problem.

Kevin Pho: So from the perspective of the EHR designers who think that physicians who complain about this are just Luddites or technophobes, as you put it, now, what is their perspective when physicians respond to this? Are a lot of them acknowledging this concern? Are they doing something about these blanket alerts, triaging them, stratifying them? What are they doing from their perspective?

Thomas Powell: So great question. So my call in the book is for exactly what you’re talking about. What I can say is there’s not been a lot of attention, because it takes a lot of work. So as I said, right now what I believe is the case in the United States is people are throwing technology undirected at things, hoping that Epic fixes it, or Cerner fixes it, or your AI product fixes it. And it’s never the technology. There’s a lot of operational clinical work that needs to happen. We actually have to buckle our belt and do some hard work, and that’s governance, and it’s decision-making, and it’s making sure there’s an owner. And so that is the hardest part of this, is that it’s so much work that it often gets abandoned. And as you said, if you’re a person who bought a $250 million electronic health record, you think it’s done, right? I mean, I’m putting it in there; it’s fixed, and why is this person complaining about the best or one of the top EHRs in the country? And it was because it wasn’t crafted for any specific purpose, especially for your local environment. That’s, I think, the key.

Kevin Pho: So tell us about the next steps in terms of stratifying and interpreting these alerts. Is it an AI problem? Is it up to someone to reinvent the workflows? Who’s the onus on in terms of solving this alert problem?

Thomas Powell: Yes, and that’s where the diagnostician is, and the diagnostician is my generic term for me for the role, because some people call it CMIO, some people call it a physician informatics leader, some people call it a CHIO. And I say the term is not the issue. What we have is a lot of names and no empowerment from the organization at all. And I say one of the best ways to see how much power a role has, not influence, is the ability to say no to something. To turn something off and to say no. And when was the last time you have seen your physician executive be able to say, “No, that’s not a good idea”? And so they’ve got to have the right staffing. They’ve got to have people with the right training. You have to realize that this is hard and heavy work, now especially in the days of AI. AI, 99 percent of AI is coming into our market completely untested in any significant way before with any particular certification. So you’re taking it in. The vendors themselves are telling you that it’s a proprietary AI model, so they’re not going to tell you if they could. Even if they could tell you what they did, they wouldn’t tell you because it’s proprietary. And so how do you govern and manage and make sure in that world? That’s an ongoing set of a lot of work. And the EHR was the same. And so if you look around and your informatics is not an army, your organization is missing to some extent what’s going on now. And so if you look at some of the most credible health systems in the country, they have now armies of informatics aimed at things, and you’re doing informatics. And that informatics is just what I said. Let’s get out there and evaluate the problems, find the problems, find the workflows, work on wellness, work on efficiency, work on all the things that work, get the data right. It’s a full-time, all-time job, and I’m trying to get that out that we have just sort of undervalued the human. We’ve spent millions on electronic health records and very little on the people who can actually tune them.

Kevin Pho: So you’re a consultant, of course, and you work with many, many health care organizations, I’m sure. Give us a story, case study, or an example of a successful addressment of this problem. How has an organization successfully managed this alert fatigue problem from your standpoint?

Thomas Powell: Yes, so I’ve spent a lot of my career as the person who had to do it, and in some organizations, they did empower. So the way that you address this is, let’s just pick, like you said, let’s narrow it to just the alert problem right now because there are many problems. But the first is data. Don’t want to get too technical, but there’s a world of metadata. And so the data is, did an alert fire? And the metadata is when and who and how many and all those other. It’s all the data that’s tied to it. We can know all that. So I’ve gone into places, and I have made sure that we have steady ongoing reports. And I see a lot of places where once you get that turned on, they just take the reports and read them and put them to the side. “Oh, yeah, we do have a problem.” Because what are you going to do about it? Well, there are algorithms of how you can work down that list. The first is separate them into important versus not important. Get rid of all your alerts that are just telling people something. An alert should be there with an action item to it. So we see that your patient looks like they’re septic, and if you believe so, I’m giving you the tools to do something about it right now. And so those are the kind of alerts. The other is put them in the frequency of being blown through. So your 96 percent that are being nearly always gone through, is it important? Is there a reason for that motion that I can fix, right? Was it just configured wrong? Is it old? Is it not quite right? Is it conflicting with something else? And what you’re going to be able to find is you can reduce the library of alerts, and then you get down to a workable world. Because I’m telling you, most people don’t even retire the alerts that came out of the box. So these vendors will pull up out of the box with a set of alerts that the nation uses in general. Their broad base of users. And whether that works real well on your data in your place, the way you do business, has really never been evaluated. So that’s the thing. It’s just targeted. Use your data. Actually have people that go in and turn things off. And when you put something new in, if ever there was a need, you’re at the. Informatics at the heart of let’s craft this to go to the right people at the right time with the right information so that they can do everything right. And so that’s really what it is, is it’s mostly been neglect, to be honest with you. Most of this has just simply been there’s stuff out of the box, and it just grows. It grows unchecked.

Kevin Pho: How difficult is it to retire an alert? Because what you’re saying sounds like common sense. Why aren’t more organizations doing what you’re doing? For instance, when you say retire an alert, how easy or difficult is it for many health care organizations?

Thomas Powell: It’s literally the flip of a switch. So an alert is a build. The build is the content and the algorithm that would kick it off, and then the connection to the orders or whatever things that you were going to do to respond. And then it becomes, it’s really a container. And that’s an alert container for all the stuff that that alert needed. And you can turn it on or turn it off.

Kevin Pho: But from a bureaucratic standpoint, is it?

Thomas Powell: Oh, that’s the. Yeah, no, then that is the key, is that everyone is afraid, right? Everyone is afraid of making things go away. Because they’re afraid that everything must be there for some really good reason. And when they understand, that is not the case. The vast majority. So that is why you do clinical governance. To me, I wanted to make this point as important as I can. If you’re in an organization like I am describing, these are not IT decisions. These are not administrative decisions. These are clinical decisions. Like every clinical thing that goes on in an organization, you need clinical ownership of an alert. If there’s nobody in your group says, “I agree with that, and I’ll be the sponsor of that alert, and when anyone has a question, I’ll be the one that you can help,” if you don’t have those kinds of things, you’ve got a mess, is what you have. So I will also turn off alerts that are not owned. So you go down, and then you have clinical people making clinical decisions. I try to be, as much as I can, the doctor to the system, and every time I would fool with primary care, for example, I would come to you, Kevin. I would say, “All right, Kevin, they’re going to fiddle with your clinic, your environment. I would like you to be point on this.” And one of the hardest things we’ve had is physician involvement. And so I do say that part, we all have a part of the problem that is going on right now. From the country, the HITECH Act, the hospitals themselves, the physicians, everything is involved in this. And one of the most key things, and I know you’ve probably heard it, if you’ve been in an electronic health record system, nobody wants to pay the physician. You’ve got nurses and other people that are actually being paid to represent their areas and do those things, and so they get relatively good governance and recognition and change management and things like this. And so physicians are still being held to their RVU, and they want them to escape for a meeting, and it’s painful, so they don’t. And then I guarantee you that in that meeting, someone is going to make a painful decision for you, and that’s the key thing. That involvement and getting your physician staff to know that, “By the way, I’m here because I’m trying to make the whole clinical system better, but for you as a physician, if you’re not there, often what’ll be passed to you is something that you don’t like.” And that’s really what’s happened, is there’s a lot of documentation that we don’t want our most expensive resource in the house wasting time on this documentation the way they did. So there’s a lot of that kind of thing that you have to get right. It’s a lot of governance, a lot of meeting and thinking and having smart people in the room with you. And then the rest is just the technical parameter, right? The next is just turning it on, turning it off.

Kevin Pho: We are talking to Thomas Powell. He’s a physician executive and a chief medical information officer. Today’s KevinMD article is “Alert fatigue is a design problem, not a vigilance problem.” Thomas, as always, let’s end with your take-home messages to the KevinMD audience.

Thomas Powell: I think you did such a good job. You led me right to that’s what it is. I mean, I think the main thing to get to the audience is when you sit down and write a book, and I started gathering. My premise was health care is sick, and I did the clinical method. I, as the physician of the organization, did the clinical method and ran down what it did and what the diagnosis is and then how you treat it. And that was the whole thing. And what you realize is America is not just a little sick. Our quality, our safety, our margin, two out of five hospital systems are now functioning in the red. It’s the money, the workforce, the burnout. All of that’s going on. It is real, and it is fixable. I was surprised at how much of these come back to just things that have never been diagnosed and treated. That’s really what it is. You diagnose it and treat it, and there may be some local variation that’s important to you, but it can be fixed. So I highly recommend that you join forces. If you’re the chair or a leader of a specialty or a leader of some other clinical aspect of your hospital, get your people in the rooms and sort of demand to speak for the clinical role, because that’s what I am trying to say, is somehow health care got away from us a little bit. And the physician in the room is an important voice, and I have one in every room, and it’s crafted to be for whose specialty makes that most important. So I highly recommend that you show. I highly recommend you participate. Now, it would be great if you loved it. It would be great if you were interested. But what I’m trying to say is, do it because without it, your organization is going to make that decision anyway. And if you’re not in the room, it will not be a decision that you probably enjoy.

Kevin Pho: Thomas, thank you so much for sharing your perspective and insight. Thanks again for coming on the show.

Thomas Powell: Thanks, Kevin.

title: Who owns the time AI clinical documentation saves?
summary: Recent health care technology headlines have celebrated something hospitals desperately need: fewer clicks. Health systems piloting ambient artificial intelligence for nursing documentation describe l...
full_content:
Recent health care technology headlines have celebrated something hospitals desperately need: fewer clicks. Health systems piloting ambient artificial intelligence for nursing documentation describe less back-charting and more time with patients. The technology is promising, though questions remain about patient experience and scaling.

Other reporting has described a more unsettling possibility: Artificial intelligence could reshape hospital work through new expectations, monitoring, and productivity pressure. Saving time on documentation does not automatically mean giving health care workers time to recover.

Reading these stories, I wondered: If AI gives a nurse ten minutes back, who gets to decide what those ten minutes are for?

I work in health care management in Taiwan while pursuing doctoral research. I have come to recognize two kinds of professional exhaustion. One comes from caring for people: discharge arrangements, staffing, difficult conversations, unexpected emergencies, and the responsibility that follows a patient home. The other comes from constantly proving that our work has value.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

For colleagues who also teach, study, or conduct research, the second burden often arrives in four short labels: Q1, Q2, Q3, and Q4. These are journal quartiles, often reported through Journal Citation Reports (JCR). A quartile ranks journals relative to others in a subject category. It does not rank the kindness of a nurse, the clinical judgment of a physician, or the importance of a problem affecting patients. Yet under promotion and institutional recognition systems, a journal-level metric can begin to feel like a verdict on a person.

I have watched how easily a practical question becomes an administrative one. A team asks whether an intervention helped older adults remain active; later, the conversation shifts to where the manuscript can be published, whether its index qualifies, and how many points it will earn. Those questions can be necessary. They are not the same as asking whether the work helped someone.

This autumn, I experienced a small version of that tension. A manuscript on AI-supported aging care was judged unsuitable for its original journal and moved into a publisher’s transfer process. The editors suggested other possible venues. Some of the options discussed were indexed only in the Emerging Sources Citation Index (ESCI).

A transfer is not acceptance, and a scope decision is not proof that the research is worthless. Still, our academic recognition requirements made the distinction consequential: A journal indexed in the Science Citation Index Expanded (SCIE) or the Social Sciences Citation Index (SSCI) could meet certain requirements, while an ESCI-only journal might not. We were considering an institutional rule, not claiming that every ESCI journal lacks scientific quality.

There is an irony here. Clarivate introduced unified JCR rankings that include ESCI journals in relevant science and social science categories. An ESCI journal may therefore have a Journal Impact Factor and a Q1 to Q4 quartile. “ESCI” is not another way of saying “Q4.” But an institution may still recognize one index and exclude another.

The manuscript had not suddenly lost its questions, its reviewers’ comments, or the hours invested by its authors. What changed was the route through which the institution might count it. I found that distinction harder to leave at the office than I expected.

Academic uncertainty resembles the quieter side of clinical work. We wait for decisions, revise in response to criticism, write careful explanations, and try not to mistake a procedural outcome for a statement about our worth. Then another deadline appears.

Against that background, I have returned to an almost unfashionable practice in the AI era: writing personal essays in the spirit of the traditional blog. Before every sentence could be optimized for search engines and generated in seconds, people used blogs to make room for experiences that did not belong in a chart, report, or promotion file. They wrote about a hard day, an unexpected kindness, an uncomfortable question, or a disappointment too small to justify a formal meeting but too persistent to forget.

The traditional blog was not always a publishing strategy. Sometimes it was a private form of attention. Writing one paragraph forced a person to ask: What actually happened? Why did it stay with me? What can I carry forward, and what can I set down?

Today, AI can help me organize ideas, check grammar, and communicate across languages. I welcome those tools. But when a machine can produce a polished reflection instantly, the danger is that we may mistake polish for processing. An elegant paragraph is not evidence that the writer has made sense of an experience.

I have published more than forty essays on KevinMD. I appreciate every opportunity to reach readers. Yet I do not want to transform that count into another quartile, another target, or another source of guilt. Not every shift needs a story; not every feeling needs an audience.

The reason to write is sometimes more modest. A difficult encounter becomes a few sentences in a notebook. A hospital colleague writes a private reflection after a demanding shift. Two coworkers discuss a piece that reminds them of an experience they have never quite found words for. The benefit, if it comes, lies in making meaning and connection rather than producing another piece of content.

Research gives this idea some support, but it calls for humility. A 2026 systematic review of expressive writing among health care professionals found potentially beneficial effects on psychological distress, while results for burnout and related outcomes were mixed. Writing may be useful for some people. It is not a cure, and it should never become a mandatory wellness exercise.

Hospitals could make space for voluntary writing groups, reflective conversations, or protected time to think. AI could serve as a language assistant rather than a substitute for experience. Staff would need clear privacy rules: no identifiable patient information, no exposing a coworker’s private struggle without permission, and no pressure to disclose personal pain to a supervisor.

More importantly, reflection cannot substitute for safe staffing, fair schedules, adequate rest, or access to confidential mental health care. No one should be expected to write beautifully about a system that refuses to change.

Hospitals are skilled at measuring admissions, discharges, encounters, citations, impact factors, and documentation time. Each measure can be useful. None tells us whether a nurse felt supported after a hard shift or whether a researcher could sleep after a disappointing decision.

Perhaps the old blog still has a role in the age of AI precisely because it does not have to function like a dashboard. It allows someone to say, in imperfect words, “That was difficult,” and to discover that another person understands.

I still believe in rigorous research and responsible publication standards. I still care about getting a manuscript into an appropriate journal. But I do not believe a journal’s quartile should determine whether a professional experience deserves to be expressed.

Q1, Q2, Q3, and Q4 classify journals, not people. ESCI describes an index, not a person’s worth. And an AI-generated draft, however fluent, cannot decide how a lived experience should matter to the person who lived it.

If technology can save clinicians thousands of clicks, I hope health care leaders will return some of that time to their people, not simply recalculate it as another productivity goal.

AI can draft what happened during a clinical encounter. The people who lived through the day are still the ones who can tell us what it meant. Sometimes the first step toward recovery is not another publication or perfectly optimized paragraph. It is simply having somewhere to write, and knowing that someone may listen.

Gerald Kuo, a PhD candidate in the Graduate Institute of Business Administration at Fu Jen Catholic University in Taiwan, specializes in health care management, long-term care systems, AI governance in clinical and social care settings, and elder care policy. He is vice chairperson of the Taiwan Home Health Care Charity Association, deputy secretary-general of the Taiwan Society of Medication, Exercise, and Nutrition for Aging, and a management specialist at the Taipei Jen-Chi Relief Institution. He maintains a professional presence on Facebook, where he shares updates on research and community work. Kuo helps operate a day-care center for older adults, working closely with families, nurses, and community physicians. His research and practical efforts focus on reducing administrative strain on clinicians, strengthening continuity and quality of elder care, and developing sustainable service models through data, technology, and cross-disciplinary collaboration. He is particularly interested in how emerging AI tools can support aging clinical workforces, enhance care delivery, and build greater trust between health systems and the public.

title: Interoperability vs. integration: what clinicians need
summary: The health care industry has spent years working toward interoperability. What we’ve accomplished to date represents significant progress, with connected devices, electronic health records, adva...
full_content:
The health care industry has spent years working toward interoperability. What we’ve accomplished to date represents significant progress, with connected devices, electronic health records, advanced monitoring systems, applications, and data repositories that once operated in isolation now increasingly working together.

For clinicians, however, those connections only matter at the bedside if they change what a care provider can see, understand, or act on. Simply moving data from one system to another does not necessarily make it easier to find, interpret, or determine what requires attention. So, while the industry has made substantial advances in interoperability, a gap still remains between connectivity and true integration, and it carries a hidden cost.

The financial burden is not always visible on a balance sheet, but clinicians experience it every day. It shows up in minutes lost, duplicate work, missed context, alert burden, and technology that is technically available but practically underused. As clinicians, we should expect more.

Pivot from asking “Can these systems connect?” to “What are these systems achieving?”

Early interoperability efforts focused on whether two systems could exchange information, and while we’ve largely proven they can, the better measure of success is what happens once the data arrives.

Real physician voices, twice a week

Free, and one click to unsubscribe.

Consider a patient whose physiologic data can be transferred from a bedside monitor into another clinical system. If the clinician still has to open multiple screens, search for the relevant trend, compare timestamps, identify which values matter, and mentally reconstruct what changed, the interface may have moved data without doing much to reduce the work required to use it.

The same is true when a hospital adds an application to solve a specific problem. A new tool may provide valuable capability, but if clinicians must learn an entirely new workflow, remember another login, or navigate even more screens and dashboards, the organization is likely adding more complexity to an already crowded environment.

Successful transmission alone is not enough. Integration should be measured by whether the technology turns information into usable clinical context.

Good integration should remove work, not shift it elsewhere

Clinicians have become accustomed to adapting to imperfect systems. They create workarounds, memorize where information lives, and ask colleagues to confirm whether another system is showing the same data. In effect, they become the human integration layer.

The danger is that this ability to adapt can make poor integration appear functional, even when the underlying workflow remains fragmented and inefficient. Nurses and physicians may learn to compensate for that fragmentation, but every added search, manual reconciliation, and unnecessary transition consumes attention that could be directed toward the patient.

That is why one of the most useful ways to evaluate integration is to ask what it eliminates. Does it remove a step? Does it reduce duplicate documentation? Does it surface relevant information within the clinician’s existing workflow? Does it provide context rather than another stream of raw data? Does it help the care team recognize an important patient change sooner? If the answer is no, it is worth asking whether the organization has integrated its technology or simply connected more technology to the clinician.

Before adding more technology, assess what you already have

Hospitals understandably look to new technology when trying to improve efficiency, address staffing pressures, or modernize care. Sometimes a new investment is exactly what is needed.

But before adding another platform, leaders should ask whether the organization is getting full value from the data and capabilities already in place. Clinical environments generate enormous amounts of information. The challenge is typically not about volume, but usability: where information resides, how it is connected and interpreted, when it reaches the right people, and whether it arrives with enough context to immediately act on.

That creates an important opportunity. Instead of beginning every improvement effort with “What should we buy?” health systems can also ask, “What are we already generating that clinicians cannot easily use?” That question can uncover gaps that are less about acquiring technology and more about connecting, configuring, or presenting existing information more effectively.

It also brings clinicians into the conversation earlier. Frontline users often know exactly where information gets stuck because they encounter those friction points every shift.

Design for the next need, not only the current one

Clinical needs continue to evolve as care models shift, patient volumes change, and hospitals introduce different devices and new digital tools. An integration strategy built only around today’s requirements can quickly become tomorrow’s constraint. For clinicians, that may mean more workarounds. For IT teams, it can mean a growing web of connections that is harder to maintain.

A more sustainable approach is to think beyond isolated interfaces and build for flexibility. Can new sources of clinical data be added without rebuilding workflows? Can information be presented consistently as systems evolve? Flexibility should be treated as both a technical and clinical priority, because infrastructure decisions ultimately shape how clinicians work.

Is technology making the clinical environment quieter or louder?

Every new system competes for clinician attention, making complexity an important clinical consideration. A well-integrated environment should make it easier to identify what matters by reducing unnecessary navigation, duplication, and the need to reconcile information across systems. Ideally, technology supports the workflow without constantly demanding attention.

A useful test is simple: Does this make the clinician’s job clearer? Can clinicians find the information they need, understand what has changed, and act without reconstructing the patient’s story across multiple systems? That is where interoperability begins to deliver real value, for patient care and the clinicians providing it.

Connectivity is just the start

Health care does not need more data; it needs to get more value from the data already surrounding the patient. That requires moving beyond a definition of integration based on whether systems can communicate. The better standard is whether that communication improves the clinician’s ability to understand the patient and make a timely, informed decision.

If data arrives but remains difficult to find, interpret, or respond to, the connection has fallen short of its clinical purpose. Systems “talking to each other” should not be the finish line. The better test is whether the right information reaches clinicians in a format they can understand, within the workflow where they need it, and without adding another layer between them and the patient.

Marilyn Flood is a health care executive.

title: “麒麟中子刀”发布一期临床结果，国产硼中子治疗癌症迈入产业化关键期
summary: 11月15日，凤麟核在青岛举行的2026中子医学战略研讨会上，正式公布其自主研发的“麒麟中子刀”一期临床试验结果。该国产硼中子俘获治疗（BNCT）系统实现了从中子源、治疗计划软件到靶向硼药的全链条自主可控，标志着我国BNCT产业从技术攻关迈入临床验证与商业化落地的关键期。作为肿瘤治疗“第五疗法”，BNCT具备细胞级精准靶向、单次短疗程及对正常组织损伤小等优势。“麒麟中子刀”依托团队40余年核技术积...
full_content:
11月15日，2026中子医学战略研讨会暨凤麟（齐鲁）高端论坛在青岛举行。

 

会上，凤麟核正式公布其自主研发的“麒麟中子刀”高端精准治疗系统一期临床试验结果，这套实现中子源、治疗计划软件、靶向硼药全链条自主可控的国产 BNCT 方案，首次交出临床有效性与安全性验证答卷，标志着国产硼中子俘获治疗产业从技术攻关阶段，正式迈入临床验证与商业化落地并行的关键周期。

 

本次会议由产学研中子治疗协同创新平台（医联体）主办。中国科学院院士、国际核能院院士、凤麟核创始人吴宜灿，中国产学研合作促进会原会长王建华，中国台湾振兴医院、台北医学大学教授颜上惠，中华医学会放射肿瘤治疗学分会副主任委员刘士新，国务院特殊津贴专家、山东大学齐鲁医院副院长、中华医学会BNCT学组组长程玉峰，中国生物医学工程学会医学物理分会主任委员邱杰等两岸专家代表300余人参会，围绕BNCT技术攻关、临床转化、药械一体化与人才体系建设四大议题展开探讨。

 

 


吴宜灿院士在主旨报告中介绍了全球BNCT发展现状和凤麟核“麒麟中子刀”的研发创新实践。

 

BNCT被称为继手术、放疗、化疗、免疫治疗之后的肿瘤治疗“第五疗法”，属于细胞级二元靶向放疗技术，凭借细胞级精准靶向、单次短疗程、对正常组织损伤小、适合多线复发难治肿瘤等突出优势（即超级精准、超短疗程、超强疗效等“三超”特点），为破解晚期实体肿瘤治疗困境提供了新手段。

 

中国科学院院士、国际核能院院士、凤麟核创始人吴宜灿

 

作为国产高端医疗装备，“麒麟中子刀”从强流加速器中子源、多物理场耦合中子治疗计划软件到靶向硼药物，全部实现自主化研发。凤麟核将40余年核聚变、核裂变及核安全领域积累的中子物理、辐射输运技术等科研成果跨界转化至放射肿瘤治疗赛道，打造出设备、软件、硼药、临床应用服务“四位一体”完整解决方案，打通从基础核科研到临床治病救人的创新链条。

 

“深耕先进核能‘核电宝’，是保障国家能源安全；研发‘麒麟中子刀’，是守护人民生命健康。两项事业，都是做有用的科研。”吴宜灿院士如此阐释团队的初心使命。

 


本次会议的核心里程碑，是“麒麟中子刀”一期临床试验数据的正式披露。

 

程玉峰教授在会上公布，本次入组患者均为经手术、放疗、化疗等多线标准治疗后失败或复发的晚期头颈部恶性肿瘤患者。初步数据显示，每位患者仅接受1次中子照射，照射时间不超过1小时，治疗3个月后观察的客观缓解率（即肿瘤明显缩小或消失的患者比例）与日本已上市获得广泛临床应用的设备疗效相当，验证了“麒麟中子刀”系统的安全性与有效性，标志着国产BNCT装备从“造得出”向“治得好”迈出关键一步。

 

截至目前，“麒麟中子刀”首台临床试验装置已在山东大学齐鲁医院建成，并依托凤麟核与山东大学齐鲁医院联合共建的凤麟核（青岛）齐鲁中子医学中心开展临床试验；首台商业应用装备落户安徽宿松，将应用于凤麟核（安庆）松兹中子医学中心，为后续规模化临床应用搭建载体。

 


“麒麟中子刀”的临床进展，是国内中子医学赛道加速发展的一个缩影。当前，行业正处于政策红利与市场需求双重驱动的发展窗口期。

 

从政策端看，发展高端医疗装备是培育生物医药领域新质生产力的关键抓手，攻克难治性肿瘤是落实健康中国战略的核心任务。工信部等十部门印发的《医药工业发展“十五五”规划》，将高端放射治疗系统列为重点攻坚方向；BNCT等放射治疗新技术被纳入国家医保局印发的《放射治疗类医疗服务价格项目立项指南（试行）》；国家药监局也将BNCT列入国家优先审批高端医疗器械目录。

 

产业端的热度同步升温。本次会议吸引了多地政府主管单位代表，北京协和医院、中国人民解放军总医院、厦门弘爱医院等医疗机构及全国30多个省份医院的代表参会；融通集团、海通恒信、盈远资本、嘉道资本、东方证券、华西证券等数十家投资机构的代表也出席了会议。

 

政产学研医资多方齐聚，反映出各方对BNCT这一新兴领域的高度期待。下一步，行业将持续以核心技术自主创新为牵引，加快完善临床诊疗规范、质量控制体系与人才培养体系，推动国产中子治疗技术普惠落地，让更多复发难治肿瘤患者用得上、用得起新一代精准抗癌疗法。同时，行业也将持续深化国际学术交流与产业合作，为世界高端医疗产业进步贡献中国智慧、中国方案。

title: 易来克®，全球首个靶向ROCK2抑制剂，寻求全国经销商
summary: 11月14日，2026创新药高质量发展大会在苏州举行，正式发布新版国家医保及商保创新药目录。新版基本医保目录新增107种药品，含51种一类创新药；商保目录新增12种药品。此次调整显示医保政策正从单一支付向研发、准入及多元支付全链条延伸，基本医保与商业健康保险协同机制持续完善，助力创新成果加速转化为临床与市场价值。赛诺菲达必妥等四适应症首进医保，默克贝捷迈等本土一类创新药亦获支持，覆盖肿瘤、罕见病等...
full_content:
11月14日，2026创新药高质量发展大会在苏州举行。会上，2026年国家基本医疗保险、生育保险和工伤保险药品目录及《商业健康保险创新药品目录》正式发布。新版基本医保目录新增107种药品，其中包括51种一类创新药；新版商保创新药目录新增12种药品。


从目录调整结果看，创新药支持力度进一步加大，基本医保与商业健康保险的协同机制也在持续完善。更值得关注的是，医保政策正在从单一的药品准入和支付，向研发、准入、临床使用和多元支付等环节延伸。对于企业而言，进入目录不仅意味着产品获得新的支付支持，也意味着创新成果有机会更快转化为临床价值和市场价值。


本次大会释放出的政策信号，与一批企业的产品进展形成呼应。从跨国药企的创新疗法持续落地，到本土企业产品矩阵逐步丰富，再到细胞与基因治疗等前沿疗法探索多元支付路径，中国创新药产业正在进入从研发突破走向临床应用、从产品上市走向商业化兑现的新阶段。



从本轮医保目录调整结果来看，跨国药企和本土创新药企均有多款产品及新增适应症获得医保支持，涉及免疫、肿瘤、罕见病、呼吸、眼科等多个领域。部分产品还通过新增适应症、支付范围优化或剂型规格补充，进一步扩大医保保障覆盖面。


赛诺菲是本轮目录调整中产品布局较为丰富的企业之一。其达必妥®（度普利尤单抗）有四项适应症首次纳入基本医保目录，涉及6岁及以上儿童和成人哮喘、成人慢性阻塞性肺疾病、结节性痒疹及大疱性类天疱疮，原有特应性皮炎适应症则完成续约。作为靶向IL-4Rα的生物制剂，达必妥此次适应症扩展，进一步拓展了其在免疫炎症性疾病领域的应用。


此外，赛诺菲还有多款创新药获得目录支持：星舒平®（阿夫凯泰）用于梗阻性肥厚型心肌病，瑞达普®（普乐司兰钠）用于家族性乳糜微粒血症综合征，安煦®（罗伐昔替尼）用于骨髓纤维化，赛菲因®（芬妥司兰钠）用于血友病，均纳入基本医保目录；可倍力®（卡拉西珠单抗）则进入商保创新药目录，用于免疫介导的血栓性血小板减少性紫癜。多款产品覆盖不同疾病领域，体现出企业在罕见病及专科治疗领域的布局。


默克方面，贝捷迈®（盐酸匹米替尼胶囊）首次纳入医保目录。该药由和誉医药研发，是中国首个且目前唯一获批用于腱鞘巨细胞瘤系统性治疗的一类创新药，于2025年12月获批。此次纳入有望进一步提升相关患者的治疗可及性。


优时比此次有两款创新药获得医保支持。倍捷乐®（比奇珠单抗）是一款靶向IL-17A和IL-17F的双靶点抑制剂，医保覆盖强直性脊柱炎、放射学阴性中轴型脊柱关节炎、斑块状银屑病及化脓性汗腺炎等适应症；优迪革®（罗泽利昔珠单抗）则是一款FcRn拮抗剂，用于抗体阳性的成人全身型重症肌无力患者，覆盖乙酰胆碱受体抗体阳性和肌肉特异性酪氨酸激酶抗体阳性人群。两款产品从不同疾病机制切入，拓展了自身免疫性疾病的治疗选择。


在眼科领域，参天制药的泰浦康®（他氟噻吗滴眼液）纳入医保目录，用于降低开角型青光眼或高眼压症患者的眼压。作为中国首个含前列腺素衍生物且不含防腐剂的原研复方制剂，该产品为青光眼患者提供了新的治疗选择，也有助于减轻长期用药的经济负担。


阿斯利康则在呼吸系统疾病领域取得进展。泰适卓®（特泽利尤单抗）是一款靶向胸腺基质淋巴细胞生成素（TSLP）的单克隆抗体，此次新增适应症涉及成人及12岁以上青少年重度哮喘维持治疗，以及成人慢性鼻窦炎伴鼻息肉，进一步拓展了其在呼吸系统疾病领域的应用。


罗氏在血液疾病和眼科领域均有产品取得医保进展。舒友立乐®（艾美赛珠单抗注射液）首次纳入基本医保目录，覆盖伴或不伴凝血因子Ⅷ抑制物的A型血友病患者规律替代治疗。该药通过模拟凝血因子Ⅷ的辅助功能帮助恢复凝血过程，并采用皮下注射方式。此次纳入也意味着成人A型血友病规律预防治疗首次获得国家医保支付支持。


眼科方面，罗视佳®（法瑞西单抗注射液）完成医保续约，支付范围进一步优化：每眼累计支付支数由最多9支调整为最多14支，预充式注射剂规格同步纳入。


从参天的青光眼治疗药物，到罗氏用于眼底疾病治疗的法瑞西单抗，本轮目录调整进一步拓展了眼科领域的医保保障范围，既覆盖不同类型的眼科疾病，也通过支付支数和剂型规格优化回应患者长期治疗需求。


与跨国药企在多个治疗领域持续拓展产品覆盖相呼应，本土创新药企也在通过原创药物研发和适应症拓展，推动更多创新成果进入医保。


云顶新耀有两款产品首次纳入基本医保目录，分别为维适平®（精氨酸艾曲莫德片）和依嘉®（注射用盐酸依拉环素），耐赋康®（布地奈德肠溶胶囊）则完成续约。其中，维适平是中国首个且唯一获批用于治疗溃疡性结肠炎的S1P受体调节剂；依嘉是一款用于复杂性腹腔感染的全合成氟环素类抗菌药。三款产品覆盖自身免疫、感染及肾脏疾病领域。


亚盛医药的利生妥®（利沙托克拉）首次纳入基本医保目录，用于既往接受过至少一种系统治疗，且治疗方案包含BTK抑制剂的成人慢性淋巴细胞白血病/小淋巴细胞淋巴瘤患者。作为中国首个上市的国产原创Bcl-2抑制剂，该药进入医保有望为相关患者提供新的治疗选择。与此同时，耐立克®（奥雷巴替尼）完成续约。作为中国首个获批上市的第三代BCR-ABL抑制剂，其持续获得医保支持，也体现出医保对国产原创药物临床价值的认可。


神基制药的艾久维®（夫瑞奈珠单抗注射液）首次纳入医保目录。该药靶向降钙素基因相关肽（CGRP）配体，用于成人偏头痛预防治疗，可采用每月一次225mg或每季度一次675mg的皮下注射方案。医保准入有望降低患者长期预防治疗的经济门槛。


翰森制药本轮有多款产品通过新增适应症、续约及首次纳入等方式获得医保支持。阿美乐®（甲磺酸阿美替尼）新增一项适应症进入医保，用于联合培美曲塞和铂类化疗药物治疗EGFR突变非小细胞肺癌一线患者，目前其已获批的五项适应症均纳入医保目录。昕越®（伊奈利珠单抗）新增IgG4相关性疾病和全身型重症肌无力两项适应症纳入医保，原有视神经脊髓炎谱系疾病适应症完成续约。此外，豪森昕福®（甲磺酸氟马替尼）和孚来美®（聚乙二醇洛塞那肽）完成续约，瑞易麟®（帕立骨化醇软胶囊）首次纳入目录。产品覆盖肿瘤、自身免疫性疾病及代谢性疾病等领域，体现出企业通过适应症拓展和产品梯队建设提升创新药可及性的路径。


诺诚健华的创新药品也出现在本轮新增谈判药品名单中，其自主研发的新一代TRK抑制剂宜诺欣®（佐来曲替尼）已被纳入新版国家医保药品目录，用于治疗携带 NTRK融合基因的成人和12岁以上青少年实体瘤患者。


随着更多国产创新药进入医保，国内药企的创新成果正加快走向更广泛的临床应用，也为产业持续发展提供新的市场空间。



在大会政策解读环节，国家医保局医药服务管理司司长黄新宇介绍了2026年医保药品目录和商保创新药目录的调整思路。国家医保局成立后，目录动态调整逐步常态化，并从海选制转向申报制，形成谈判、竞价、续约等机制。


今年目录调整进一步优化规则：建立参照药预沟通机制，已完成两批59个参照药沟通，绝大部分预沟通结果与专家评审一致；建立商保目录与基本医保目录衔接机制，两款商保药品成功转入基本医保，并保留相关支付政策；完善申报条件，对附条件上市后近三年转为常规批准、商保目录药品转基本医保、原研未续约后同通用名仿制药申报等情形作出安排。


可以发现从目录准入到落地使用，医保政策释放了一些新信号：首先，目录调整机制进一步精细化，企业申报预期更加明确。


本轮目录调整新增药品的申报条件有所优化。在原有申报条件基础上，新增了三类情形：一是2020年以后附条件批准上市、且近三年内转为常规批准的药品，可以获得额外申报机会；二是已经进入商保创新药目录的药品，符合条件后可以申请进入基本医保目录，不再受固定时间限制；三是原研药曾经进入医保目录但未能续约的，其同通用名仿制药在符合条件时仍有机会申报。


这些调整分别回应了创新药研发和上市过程中可能遇到的实际问题。对于附条件批准的药品，政策为其补充临床证据、转为常规批准后争取医保准入留出了空间；对于已经进入商保目录的药品，则进一步畅通了向基本医保衔接的路径；对于仿制药申报资格的调整，也体现出目录管理规则对不同市场情形的考虑。


与此同时，本轮目录调整还首次建立参照药预沟通机制。黄新宇介绍，今年已完成两批共59个参照药预沟通，预沟通结果与专家实际评审结果的一致率达到97%。这一机制有助于企业提前了解参照药选择及相关评价思路，减少申报过程中的不确定性，也使目录评审更加规范、透明。


其次，基本医保与商保目录之间的衔接进一步加强。


商保目录的定位并不是替代基本医保，也不是要求商业保险机构必须纳入目录中的所有药品。黄新宇在解读中强调，商保目录不是强制性目录，商业健康保险机构仍然根据自身产品定位和风险管理需要，自主确定保障范围。医保部门更多是通过目录提供参考，并配套政策支持，推动商业保险资金更有效地用于具有临床价值的创新药。


本轮政策进一步明确，商保目录内药品符合条件后，可以申请进入基本医保目录，且不再受固定时间限制。对于已经从商保目录转入基本医保的药品，医保部门也考虑了临床使用的连续性，在相关协议期内保留必要的支付政策安排，减少目录转换对临床使用造成的影响。


这意味着，商保目录不仅为创新药提供了基本医保之外的补充支付渠道，也有望成为部分创新药进入基本医保前的探索路径。不过，能否进入基本医保，仍需满足相应的临床价值和价格等要求，并非进入商保目录后就自动转入。


再次，医保谈判与集中带量采购的功能边界需要进一步厘清。


政策解读会中，黄新宇特别强调，医保目录谈判与集中带量采购并不是一回事。医保谈判主要围绕医保支付标准和保障范围展开，并不直接承诺采购数量；集中带量采购则有独立的采购规则和目标。两者在政策功能和运行机制上有所区别。


这一说明对创新药企业尤为重要。医保准入意味着药品获得医保支付支持，但并不等同于获得采购量承诺。企业仍需要结合产品临床价值、市场需求和医疗机构使用情况，做好准入后的市场规划。同时，医保基金承受能力也是目录调整必须考虑的因素，创新药获得支持与医保基金可持续运行需要统筹平衡。


最后，政策支持正从目录准入进一步延伸到临床使用和支付落地。


目录公布并不意味着创新药已经自动进入所有医疗机构。如何推动医院配备、促进临床合理使用，以及让商保折扣真正落实，仍是目录落地的重要环节。


黄新宇介绍，医保部门计划在12个省区市开展医药保学面对面交流活动，为企业与医疗机构之间搭建合规沟通平台，帮助医院了解创新药的临床价值和使用信息。同时，针对商保目录落地过程中企业与保险机构反映的折扣兑现问题，政策也提出更加灵活的处理方式：只要企业与保险机构认可具体方案，并向医保部门说明，协商折扣可以通过不同方式体现，以降低双方实际落地的操作压力。


此外，真实世界研究也成为医保部门鼓励探索的方向。通过积累真实临床使用数据，可以进一步评价药品的有效性、安全性和经济性，为医保决策及创新药价值评价提供更多证据。


整体来看，2026年医保目录调整的变化，不仅体现在新增药品数量和覆盖领域上，更体现在制度机制的持续完善。从参照药预沟通到申报条件优化，从商保与基本医保衔接到目录落地服务，政策支持正在覆盖创新药从准入到临床使用的更多环节。


对创新药行业而言，未来竞争不仅是研发和获批速度的竞争，也将更加考验产品能否体现明确的临床价值、能否形成合理的支付方案，以及能否真正进入医疗机构并惠及患者。基本医保与商业健康保险协同发展的多层次保障体系，也将为创新药从研发成果走向临床可及提供更丰富的路径。
